Their communication and boundaries matter when predicting where fluid, blood or infection may collect. These spaces are potential compartments connected by defined routes rather than completely sealed cavities. Their boundaries and dependent positions help explain where fluid or infection may accumulate on CT or ultrasound.

questions.chapterTitle: The anterior abdominal wall and peritoneum
questions.question: Which structure forms the principal communication between the greater and lesser sacs?
questions.explanation: Correct answer: C. The epiploic foramen connects the greater sac to the lesser sac. Its position behind the free edge of the lesser omentum is important when describing the spaces around the liver and upper abdomen. These spaces are potential compartments connected by defined routes rather than completely sealed cavities. Their boundaries and dependent positions help explain where fluid or infection may accumulate on CT or ultrasound.

questions.chapterTitle: The anterior abdominal wall and peritoneum
questions.question: Which ligament forms the anterior boundary of the epiploic foramen?
questions.explanation: Correct answer: D. The hepatoduodenal ligament, the thickened free right edge of the lesser omentum, lies anterior to the epiploic foramen. The inferior vena cava lies posteriorly, the caudate lobe superiorly, and the duodenum inferiorly. These spaces are potential compartments connected by defined routes rather than completely sealed cavities. Their boundaries and dependent positions help explain where fluid or infection may accumulate on CT or ultrasound.

questions.chapterTitle: The anterior abdominal wall and peritoneum
questions.question: Which major vessel lies posterior to the epiploic foramen?
questions.explanation: Correct answer: D. The inferior vena cava forms the posterior boundary of the epiploic foramen. Anteriorly is the hepatoduodenal ligament, superiorly the caudate lobe, and inferiorly the first part of the duodenum. These spaces are potential compartments connected by defined routes rather than completely sealed cavities. Their boundaries and dependent positions help explain where fluid or infection may accumulate on CT or ultrasound.

questions.chapterTitle: The anterior abdominal wall and peritoneum
questions.question: Which liver region forms the superior boundary of the epiploic foramen?
questions.explanation: Correct answer: B. The caudate lobe lies superior to the epiploic foramen. Knowing these boundaries is useful on axial CT when identifying the communication between the greater and lesser sacs. These spaces are potential compartments connected by defined routes rather than completely sealed cavities. Their boundaries and dependent positions help explain where fluid or infection may accumulate on CT or ultrasound.

questions.chapterTitle: The anterior abdominal wall and peritoneum
questions.question: Which structure forms the inferior boundary of the epiploic foramen?
questions.explanation: Correct answer: A. The first part of the duodenum lies inferior to the epiploic foramen. This is distinct from the transverse colon, which is lower in the abdominal cavity and associated with the transverse mesocolon. These spaces are potential compartments connected by defined routes rather than completely sealed cavities. Their boundaries and dependent positions help explain where fluid or infection may accumulate on CT or ultrasound.

questions.chapterTitle: The anterior abdominal wall and peritoneum
questions.question: What does the lesser omentum connect?

options.text: Liver to the lesser curvature of the stomach and proximal duodenum

correctAnswer.text: Liver to the lesser curvature of the stomach and proximal duodenum

questions.explanation: Correct answer: D. The lesser omentum extends between the liver and the lesser curvature of the stomach and proximal duodenum. Its free right edge is thickened as the hepatoduodenal ligament, an important boundary of the epiploic foramen. The named folds are not interchangeable: each has a characteristic attachment and content, which is the most reliable way to identify it on cross-sectional imaging.

questions.chapterTitle: The anterior abdominal wall and peritoneum
questions.question: Which ligament is the thickened free right edge of the lesser omentum?
questions.explanation: Correct answer: D. The hepatoduodenal ligament is the free right margin of the lesser omentum and extends between the duodenum and porta hepatis. It is clinically important because it contains the portal triad and forms the anterior boundary of the epiploic foramen. The named folds are not interchangeable: each has a characteristic attachment and content, which is the most reliable way to identify it on cross-sectional imaging.

questions.chapterTitle: The anterior abdominal wall and peritoneum
questions.question: Which ligament extends from the greater curvature of the stomach to the spleen?
questions.explanation: Correct answer: D. The gastrosplenic ligament joins the greater curvature of the stomach to the splenic hilum and contains the short gastric and left gastroepiploic vessels. It is continuous with the greater omentum. The named folds are not interchangeable: each has a characteristic attachment and content, which is the most reliable way to identify it on cross-sectional imaging.

questions.chapterTitle: The anterior abdominal wall and peritoneum
questions.question: Which vessels run within the gastrosplenic ligament?

options.text: Short gastric and left gastroepiploic vessels

correctAnswer.text: Short gastric and left gastroepiploic vessels

questions.explanation: Correct answer: D. The gastrosplenic ligament carries the short gastric vessels and left gastroepiploic vessels. This is important during surgery or when tracing vascular structures near the gastric fundus and splenic hilum. The named folds are not interchangeable: each has a characteristic attachment and content, which is the most reliable way to identify it on cross-sectional imaging.

questions.chapterTitle: The anterior abdominal wall and peritoneum
questions.question: Which ligament extends from the pancreatic tail to the splenic hilum?
questions.explanation: Correct answer: C. The splenorenal ligament extends from the pancreatic tail to the splenic hilum and carries the splenic vessels. It is continuous with the gastrosplenic ligament and contributes to the left lateral boundary of the lesser sac. The named folds are not interchangeable: each has a characteristic attachment and content, which is the most reliable way to identify it on cross-sectional imaging.

questions.chapterTitle: The anterior abdominal wall and peritoneum
questions.question: Which ligament carries the splenic vessels?
questions.explanation: Correct answer: B. The splenic vessels pass within the splenorenal ligament as they travel between the pancreatic tail and splenic hilum. This relationship helps explain why the pancreatic tail is closely associated with the splenic hilum. The named folds are not interchangeable: each has a characteristic attachment and content, which is the most reliable way to identify it on cross-sectional imaging.

questions.chapterTitle: The anterior abdominal wall and peritoneum
questions.question: What does the falciform ligament connect?

options.text: The anterosuperior surface of the liver to the anterior abdominal wall and diaphragm

correctAnswer.text: The anterosuperior surface of the liver to the anterior abdominal wall and diaphragm

questions.explanation: Correct answer: D. The falciform ligament attaches the liver to the anterior abdominal wall and diaphragm. It is a peritoneal fold and is continuous inferiorly with the fissure for the ligamentum teres, a remnant of the umbilical vein. The named folds are not interchangeable: each has a characteristic attachment and content, which is the most reliable way to identify it on cross-sectional imaging.

questions.chapterTitle: The anterior abdominal wall and peritoneum
questions.question: The falciform ligament is continuous inferiorly with the fissure for which structure?

options.text: Ligamentum teres (round ligament of the liver)

correctAnswer.text: Ligamentum teres (round ligament of the liver)

questions.explanation: Correct answer: B. The falciform ligament is continuous with the fissure for the ligamentum teres. The ligamentum teres is the postnatal remnant of the umbilical vein; it should not be confused with the ligamentum venosum, the remnant of the ductus venosus. The named folds are not interchangeable: each has a characteristic attachment and content, which is the most reliable way to identify it on cross-sectional imaging.

questions.chapterTitle: The anterior abdominal wall and peritoneum
questions.question: Which ligament supports the spleen from below and extends from the splenic flexure to the diaphragm?
questions.explanation: Correct answer: C. The phrenicocolic ligament extends from the splenic flexure to the diaphragm and provides support beneath the spleen. It may also act as a partial barrier to spread of infected fluid between the left paracolic gutter and left subphrenic space. The named folds are not interchangeable: each has a characteristic attachment and content, which is the most reliable way to identify it on cross-sectional imaging.

questions.chapterTitle: The anterior abdominal wall and peritoneum
questions.question: Which peritoneal fold may impede spread of infected fluid toward the left subphrenic space?
questions.explanation: Correct answer: D. The phrenicocolic ligament lies between the splenic flexure and diaphragm and can act as a potential barrier to fluid spread into the left subphrenic region. It does not completely isolate spaces, but it influences pathways of peritoneal disease. These spaces are potential compartments connected by defined routes rather than completely sealed cavities. Their boundaries and dependent positions help explain where fluid or infection may accumulate on CT or ultrasound.

questions.chapterTitle: The anterior abdominal wall and peritoneum
questions.question: What is the right coronary ligament related to?

options.text: Root of the small bowel mesentery
Attachment of the stomach to spleen
Peritoneal reflections around the bare area of the liver

correctAnswer.text: Peritoneal reflections around the bare area of the liver

questions.explanation: Correct answer: D. The right coronary ligament is formed by peritoneal reflections around the liver’s bare area. The bare area itself lacks peritoneal covering, so the reflections mark its boundaries rather than covering it completely. The named folds are not interchangeable: each has a characteristic attachment and content, which is the most reliable way to identify it on cross-sectional imaging.

questions.chapterTitle: The anterior abdominal wall and peritoneum
questions.question: Which region of the liver is not covered by peritoneum and is associated with the coronary ligaments?
questions.explanation: Correct answer: C. The bare area is a region of the liver in direct contact with the diaphragm without intervening peritoneum. The peritoneal reflections around it form the coronary and triangular ligament regions. The named folds are not interchangeable: each has a characteristic attachment and content, which is the most reliable way to identify it on cross-sectional imaging.

questions.chapterTitle: The anterior abdominal wall and peritoneum
questions.question: What is the principal role of the small-bowel mesentery?

options.text: It anchors the liver to the diaphragm
It forms the posterior rectus sheath
It connects the stomach to the spleen
It suspends jejunum and ileum from the posterior abdominal wall and carries their neurovascular supply

correctAnswer.text: It suspends jejunum and ileum from the posterior abdominal wall and carries their neurovascular supply

questions.explanation: Correct answer: D. The small-bowel mesentery suspends the jejunum and ileum and contains fat, arterial branches from the superior mesenteric artery, accompanying veins, nerves and lymphatics. Its root is short and oblique despite the long mobile bowel it supports. A mesentery suspends bowel and provides a route for vessels, nerves and lymphatics. The small-bowel mesentery, transverse mesocolon, sigmoid mesocolon and mesoappendix are distinguished by the bowel segment each supports.

questions.chapterTitle: The anterior abdominal wall and peritoneum
questions.question: Approximately how long is the root of the small-bowel mesentery described in the chapter?
questions.explanation: Correct answer: A. The chapter describes an approximately 15 cm oblique root extending from the duodenojejunal flexure to the ileocaecal valve. This short root supports a much longer length of mobile jejunum and ileum. A mesentery suspends bowel and provides a route for vessels, nerves and lymphatics. The small-bowel mesentery, transverse mesocolon, sigmoid mesocolon and mesoappendix are distinguished by the bowel segment each supports.

questions.chapterTitle: The anterior abdominal wall and peritoneum
questions.question: Between which points does the root of the small-bowel mesentery extend?
questions.explanation: Correct answer: A. The root of the small-bowel mesentery extends obliquely from the duodenojejunal flexure to the ileocaecal valve. This orientation is important when mapping mesenteric vessels and interpreting internal hernias or mesenteric pathology. A mesentery suspends bowel and provides a route for vessels, nerves and lymphatics. The small-bowel mesentery, transverse mesocolon, sigmoid mesocolon and mesoappendix are distinguished by the bowel segment each supports.

questions.chapterTitle: The anterior abdominal wall and peritoneum
questions.question: Which artery supplies branches that travel within the small-bowel mesentery?

options.text: Coeliac trunk directly to all jejunal loops

questions.explanation: Correct answer: C. The mesentery contains jejunal and ileal branches of the superior mesenteric artery, along with accompanying veins, nerves and lymphatics. The inferior mesenteric artery primarily supplies hindgut structures rather than the jejunum and ileum. A mesentery suspends bowel and provides a route for vessels, nerves and lymphatics. The small-bowel mesentery, transverse mesocolon, sigmoid mesocolon and mesoappendix are distinguished by the bowel segment each supports.

questions.chapterTitle: The anterior abdominal wall and peritoneum
questions.question: Which mesentery attaches the transverse colon to the posterior abdominal wall?
questions.explanation: Correct answer: D. The transverse mesocolon suspends the transverse colon from the posterior abdominal wall and carries the middle colic vessels, nerves and lymphatics. It is distinct from the small-bowel mesentery and sigmoid mesocolon. A mesentery suspends bowel and provides a route for vessels, nerves and lymphatics. The small-bowel mesentery, transverse mesocolon, sigmoid mesocolon and mesoappendix are distinguished by the bowel segment each supports.

questions.chapterTitle: The anterior abdominal wall and peritoneum
questions.question: Which vessels travel in the transverse mesocolon?
questions.explanation: Correct answer: A. The transverse mesocolon contains the middle colic vessels, autonomic nerves and lymphatics supplying the transverse colon. This relationship is relevant when tracing the transverse mesocolon on CT or planning surgery. A mesentery suspends bowel and provides a route for vessels, nerves and lymphatics. The small-bowel mesentery, transverse mesocolon, sigmoid mesocolon and mesoappendix are distinguished by the bowel segment each supports.

questions.chapterTitle: The anterior abdominal wall and peritoneum
questions.question: What is the characteristic shape of the sigmoid mesocolon attachment?

options.text: A horizontal ring around the duodenum

questions.explanation: Correct answer: C. The sigmoid mesocolon attaches the sigmoid colon to the pelvic wall in an inverted V. Its apex lies anterior to the bifurcation of the left common iliac artery and the left ureter, making those structures useful landmarks. A mesentery suspends bowel and provides a route for vessels, nerves and lymphatics. The small-bowel mesentery, transverse mesocolon, sigmoid mesocolon and mesoappendix are distinguished by the bowel segment each supports.

questions.chapterTitle: The anterior abdominal wall and peritoneum
questions.question: Where is the apex of the inverted-V sigmoid mesocolon root located?

options.text: Anterior to the left common iliac artery bifurcation and left ureter

correctAnswer.text: Anterior to the left common iliac artery bifurcation and left ureter

questions.explanation: Correct answer: D. The apex of the sigmoid mesocolon root is positioned anterior to the left common iliac artery bifurcation and left ureter. These relationships matter because the ureter may be at risk during pelvic surgery. A mesentery suspends bowel and provides a route for vessels, nerves and lymphatics. The small-bowel mesentery, transverse mesocolon, sigmoid mesocolon and mesoappendix are distinguished by the bowel segment each supports.

questions.chapterTitle: The anterior abdominal wall and peritoneum
questions.question: What does the mesoappendix enclose and attach?

options.text: The vermiform appendix to the lower end of the small-bowel mesentery near the ileocaecal junction
The transverse colon to the pancreas
The liver to the anterior wall

correctAnswer.text: The vermiform appendix to the lower end of the small-bowel mesentery near the ileocaecal junction

questions.explanation: Correct answer: A. The mesoappendix surrounds the appendix and attaches near the ileocaecal junction to the lower end of the small-bowel mesentery. It usually extends to the appendiceal tip and carries the appendicular vessels. A mesentery suspends bowel and provides a route for vessels, nerves and lymphatics. The small-bowel mesentery, transverse mesocolon, sigmoid mesocolon and mesoappendix are distinguished by the bowel segment each supports.

questions.chapterTitle: The anterior abdominal wall and peritoneum
questions.question: Which peritoneal fold is associated with the appendicular vessels?
questions.explanation: Correct answer: C. The mesoappendix is the mesentery of the vermiform appendix and contains its vascular supply. Identifying this fold helps understand the appendicular blood supply and the anatomical spread of inflammation. A mesentery suspends bowel and provides a route for vessels, nerves and lymphatics. The small-bowel mesentery, transverse mesocolon, sigmoid mesocolon and mesoappendix are distinguished by the bowel segment each supports.

questions.chapterTitle: The anterior abdominal wall and peritoneum
questions.question: What determines the subdivision of the pelvic peritoneal spaces?
questions.explanation: Correct answer: C. The chapter notes that the urinary bladder subdivides the pelvis into right and left potential spaces. The exact spaces available for fluid depend on sex-specific pelvic peritoneal reflections and the position of pelvic organs. Pelvic recesses are defined by the organs between which the peritoneum reflects. Their position, especially the dependent rectouterine pouch in women, is important when searching for free fluid.

questions.chapterTitle: The anterior abdominal wall and peritoneum
questions.question: In a man, how many principal potential peritoneal spaces for fluid are described in the pelvis?
questions.explanation: Correct answer: A. In males, the chapter describes one principal potential space for pelvic fluid. This differs from the female pelvis, where the uterus creates anterior and posterior dependent recesses. Pelvic recesses are defined by the organs between which the peritoneum reflects. Their position, especially the dependent rectouterine pouch in women, is important when searching for free fluid.

questions.chapterTitle: The anterior abdominal wall and peritoneum
questions.question: In a woman, which two pelvic potential spaces are highlighted for fluid accumulation?

options.text: The right and left subphrenic spaces
The lesser sac and greater sac

questions.explanation: Correct answer: B. The uterus creates a vesicouterine pouch anteriorly and a rectouterine pouch posteriorly. The rectouterine pouch (pouch of Douglas) is often the most dependent pelvic peritoneal recess in a woman when upright. Pelvic recesses are defined by the organs between which the peritoneum reflects. Their position, especially the dependent rectouterine pouch in women, is important when searching for free fluid.

questions.chapterTitle: The anterior abdominal wall and peritoneum
questions.question: Which pelvic recess lies between the uterus and rectum?
questions.explanation: Correct answer: A. The rectouterine pouch is posterior to the uterus and anterior to the rectum. It is a dependent peritoneal recess and can collect fluid, blood or pus, which may be detected by pelvic ultrasound or CT. Pelvic recesses are defined by the organs between which the peritoneum reflects. Their position, especially the dependent rectouterine pouch in women, is important when searching for free fluid.

questions.chapterTitle: The anterior abdominal wall and peritoneum
questions.question: Which pelvic recess lies between the urinary bladder and uterus?
questions.explanation: Correct answer: C. The vesicouterine pouch is formed by peritoneal reflection between the bladder and uterus. It is anterior to the uterus, whereas the rectouterine pouch lies posteriorly between the uterus and rectum. Pelvic recesses are defined by the organs between which the peritoneum reflects. Their position, especially the dependent rectouterine pouch in women, is important when searching for free fluid.

questions.chapterTitle: The anterior abdominal wall and peritoneum
questions.question: Which peritoneal space is also known as the pouch of Douglas?
questions.explanation: Correct answer: A. The pouch of Douglas is another name for the rectouterine pouch. Its dependent position makes it a common location for pelvic fluid in women, though distribution also depends on patient position and the source of fluid. Pelvic recesses are defined by the organs between which the peritoneum reflects. Their position, especially the dependent rectouterine pouch in women, is important when searching for free fluid.

questions.chapterTitle: The anterior abdominal wall and peritoneum
questions.question: Which space lies between the liver and right hemidiaphragm?
questions.explanation: Correct answer: B. The right subphrenic space lies between the liver and right diaphragm. It is one of the important upper abdominal spaces assessed on CT for fluid or infection. These spaces are potential compartments connected by defined routes rather than completely sealed cavities. Their boundaries and dependent positions help explain where fluid or infection may accumulate on CT or ultrasound.

questions.chapterTitle: The anterior abdominal wall and peritoneum
questions.question: Which space is located inferior to the liver and superior to the right kidney region?
questions.explanation: Correct answer: A. The right subhepatic space lies beneath the liver and includes the hepatorenal recess. Fluid can collect here, particularly in a supine patient, making it an important location to inspect on abdominal imaging. These spaces are potential compartments connected by defined routes rather than completely sealed cavities. Their boundaries and dependent positions help explain where fluid or infection may accumulate on CT or ultrasound.

questions.chapterTitle: The anterior abdominal wall and peritoneum
questions.question: What is another name for the right posterior subhepatic recess?
questions.explanation: Correct answer: D. The hepatorenal recess, commonly called Morison pouch, lies between the liver and right kidney. It is a dependent upper abdominal recess in supine patients and is routinely assessed when searching for free fluid. These spaces are potential compartments connected by defined routes rather than completely sealed cavities. Their boundaries and dependent positions help explain where fluid or infection may accumulate on CT or ultrasound.

questions.chapterTitle: The anterior abdominal wall and peritoneum
questions.question: Which peritoneal space lies behind the stomach?
questions.explanation: Correct answer: A. The lesser sac lies posterior to the stomach and lesser omentum and anterior to structures such as the pancreas. It is a potential space where fluid may collect in pancreatitis or other upper abdominal disease. These spaces are potential compartments connected by defined routes rather than completely sealed cavities. Their boundaries and dependent positions help explain where fluid or infection may accumulate on CT or ultrasound.

questions.chapterTitle: The anterior abdominal wall and peritoneum
questions.question: Which organ is a key posterior relation of the lesser sac?
questions.explanation: Correct answer: C. The pancreas forms an important posterior relation to the lesser sac, with the stomach anteriorly. This explains why pancreatic inflammation or collections can communicate with or occupy the lesser sac. These spaces are potential compartments connected by defined routes rather than completely sealed cavities. Their boundaries and dependent positions help explain where fluid or infection may accumulate on CT or ultrasound.

questions.chapterTitle: The anterior abdominal wall and peritoneum
questions.question: Which spaces are separated by the transverse mesocolon?
questions.explanation: Correct answer: A. The transverse mesocolon divides the peritoneal cavity into supramesocolic and inframesocolic regions. This division helps describe the distribution of fluid, with the liver, stomach and spleen largely above and much of the small bowel below. These spaces are potential compartments connected by defined routes rather than completely sealed cavities. Their boundaries and dependent positions help explain where fluid or infection may accumulate on CT or ultrasound.

questions.chapterTitle: The anterior abdominal wall and peritoneum
questions.question: What is the right paracolic gutter?

options.text: A space between uterus and rectum
A longitudinal peritoneal channel lateral to the ascending colon
A fold between liver and anterior wall

correctAnswer.text: A longitudinal peritoneal channel lateral to the ascending colon

questions.explanation: Correct answer: C. The right paracolic gutter runs lateral to the ascending colon and provides a route along which peritoneal fluid can move between lower and upper abdominal regions. It is usually more freely communicating than the left gutter. These spaces are potential compartments connected by defined routes rather than completely sealed cavities. Their boundaries and dependent positions help explain where fluid or infection may accumulate on CT or ultrasound.

questions.chapterTitle: The anterior abdominal wall and peritoneum
questions.question: Which structure is lateral to the left paracolic gutter?

options.text: Descending colon lies medial to the gutter, with the lateral abdominal wall beyond it

correctAnswer.text: Descending colon lies medial to the gutter, with the lateral abdominal wall beyond it

questions.explanation: Correct answer: A. The left paracolic gutter is the channel lateral to the descending colon. Its relation to the phrenicocolic ligament can limit direct spread superiorly toward the left subphrenic space. These spaces are potential compartments connected by defined routes rather than completely sealed cavities. Their boundaries and dependent positions help explain where fluid or infection may accumulate on CT or ultrasound.

questions.chapterTitle: The anterior abdominal wall and peritoneum
questions.question: Why may fluid spread more freely up the right paracolic gutter than the left?

options.text: The right gutter contains no peritoneum
The left gutter is inside the rectus sheath
The left phrenicocolic ligament partly limits superior communication on the left

correctAnswer.text: The left phrenicocolic ligament partly limits superior communication on the left

questions.explanation: Correct answer: C. The phrenicocolic ligament near the splenic flexure can act as a partial barrier to upward movement from the left paracolic gutter. There is no equivalent barrier of the same significance on the right, so right-sided pathways may allow freer communication. These spaces are potential compartments connected by defined routes rather than completely sealed cavities. Their boundaries and dependent positions help explain where fluid or infection may accumulate on CT or ultrasound.

questions.chapterTitle: The anterior abdominal wall and peritoneum
questions.question: Which space is located between the liver and the right hemidiaphragm, adjacent to the bare area region?
questions.explanation: Correct answer: B. The right subphrenic space lies under the right diaphragm and above the liver. The bare area itself is not peritoneally covered, but the adjacent peritoneal spaces and reflections are important when localizing upper abdominal fluid. These spaces are potential compartments connected by defined routes rather than completely sealed cavities. Their boundaries and dependent positions help explain where fluid or infection may accumulate on CT or ultrasound.

questions.chapterTitle: The anterior abdominal wall and peritoneum
questions.question: Which description best defines a peritoneal ligament?

options.text: A fibrous band within a skeletal muscle
A vessel running in the retroperitoneum
A peritoneal fold connecting one organ to another or to the body wall

correctAnswer.text: A peritoneal fold connecting one organ to another or to the body wall

questions.explanation: Correct answer: D. Peritoneal ligaments are folds of peritoneum that connect organs to other organs or to the body wall. questions.chapterTitle: The anterior abdominal wall and peritoneum
questions.question: What is an omentum in the terminology used by the chapter?

options.text: A muscle of the lateral abdominal wall
A peritoneal fold connecting the stomach to another structure
A layer of the rectus sheath

correctAnswer.text: A peritoneal fold connecting the stomach to another structure

questions.chapterTitle: The anterior abdominal wall and peritoneum
questions.question: Which structure is formed by two layers of peritoneum enclosing fat and neurovascular structures and suspending bowel?

questions.chapterTitle: The anterior abdominal wall and peritoneum
questions.question: Which portion of the small bowel is suspended by the small-bowel mesentery?

questions.chapterTitle: The anterior abdominal wall and peritoneum
questions.question: What is the approximate length of jejunum and ileum suspended by the small-bowel mesentery in the chapter?

A mesentery suspends bowel and provides a route for vessels, nerves and lymphatics. questions.chapterTitle: The anterior abdominal wall and peritoneum
questions.question: Which vessels are associated with the greater omentum near the transverse colon?

options.text: Gastroepiploic vessels along the greater curvature region

correctAnswer.text: Gastroepiploic vessels along the greater curvature region

The named folds are not interchangeable: each has a characteristic attachment and content, which is the most reliable way to identify it on cross-sectional imaging.

questions.chapterTitle: The anterior abdominal wall and peritoneum
questions.question: What is the relationship between the greater omentum and transverse mesocolon described in the chapter?

options.text: The transverse mesocolon is continuous with Scarpa’s fascia
The upper layer of transverse mesocolon is adherent to but separable from the greater omentum
They are the same structure with no tissue plane
The greater omentum lies inside rectus abdominis

correctAnswer.text: The upper layer of transverse mesocolon is adherent to but separable from the greater omentum

questions.explanation: Correct answer: B. The chapter notes that the upper layer of the transverse mesocolon is adherent to, but separable from, the greater omentum. This is an important anatomical plane in the upper abdomen and helps distinguish related peritoneal folds. A mesentery suspends bowel and provides a route for vessels, nerves and lymphatics. The small-bowel mesentery, transverse mesocolon, sigmoid mesocolon and mesoappendix are distinguished by the bowel segment each supports.

questions.chapterTitle: The anterior abdominal wall and peritoneum
questions.question: Near which pancreatic region does the root of the transverse mesocolon become confluent with the small-bowel mesenteric root?

options.text: Near the uncinate process of the pancreas

correctAnswer.text: Near the uncinate process of the pancreas

questions.explanation: Correct answer: D. The transverse mesocolon root becomes confluent with the root of the small-bowel mesentery near the uncinate process of the pancreas. This relationship is useful when interpreting the mesenteric root and adjacent vessels on CT. A mesentery suspends bowel and provides a route for vessels, nerves and lymphatics. The small-bowel mesentery, transverse mesocolon, sigmoid mesocolon and mesoappendix are distinguished by the bowel segment each supports.

questions.chapterTitle: The anterior abdominal wall and peritoneum
questions.question: Which ligament forms the medial margin of the femoral ring?
questions.explanation: Correct answer: C. The chapter identifies the lacunar ligament as the medial part of the inguinal ligament and the medial margin of the femoral ring. This is a key relationship in understanding the femoral canal and femoral hernias. The inguinal ligament and superficial ring are related but distinct landmarks: the ligament is the thickened inferior edge of the external oblique aponeurosis, while the superficial ring is an opening in that aponeurosis.

questions.chapterTitle: The anterior abdominal wall and peritoneum
questions.question: Which nerve is specifically mentioned as passing through the superficial inguinal ring region with the cord or round ligament?
questions.explanation: Correct answer: D. The chapter notes that the superficial inguinal ring transmits the spermatic cord in males or round ligament in females and the ilioinguinal nerve. The femoral and obturator nerves follow different routes in the pelvis and thigh. The inguinal ligament and superficial ring are related but distinct landmarks: the ligament is the thickened inferior edge of the external oblique aponeurosis, while the superficial ring is an opening in that aponeurosis.

questions.chapterTitle: The anterior abdominal wall and peritoneum
questions.question: Which modality is useful for focal masses of the anterior abdominal wall but gives less anatomical relationship detail than CT or MRI?
questions.explanation: Correct answer: D. Ultrasound is useful for targeted assessment of focal abdominal wall masses, especially superficial lesions. However, the chapter states that CT and MRI better demonstrate the broader anatomical relationships and deep extent. For comparison, plain radiographs provide little direct detail of peritoneal reflections; ultrasound can be limited by gas and body habitus; CT is strong for cross-sectional mapping, while MRI offers soft-tissue contrast but can be motion-sensitive.

questions.chapterTitle: The anterior abdominal wall and peritoneum
questions.question: Which imaging statement about peritoneal assessment is most accurate according to the chapter?

options.text: Plain radiography is the preferred test for peritoneal reflections
MRI is unaffected by peristalsis or respiration
Ultrasound always shows all spaces despite bowel gas
Cross-sectional imaging is optimal for assessing the abdominal wall and peritoneum

correctAnswer.text: Cross-sectional imaging is optimal for assessing the abdominal wall and peritoneum

questions.explanation: Correct answer: D. The chapter emphasizes cross-sectional techniques for assessing the anterior abdominal wall and peritoneum. CT is the method of choice for peritoneal spaces and contents; MRI provides useful soft-tissue detail but may be affected by motion, while ultrasound can be limited by gas and habitus. For comparison, plain radiographs provide little direct detail of peritoneal reflections; ultrasound can be limited by gas and body habitus; CT is strong for cross-sectional mapping, while MRI offers soft-tissue contrast but can be motion-sensitive.

questions.chapterTitle: The anterior abdominal wall and peritoneum
questions.question: What is the principal content carried by the hepatoduodenal ligament in addition to its peritoneal role?

options.text: Splenic vessels and short gastric arteries

questions.explanation: Correct answer: D. The hepatoduodenal ligament is the thickened free edge of the lesser omentum and contains the portal triad: portal vein, proper hepatic artery and bile duct. The chapter emphasizes its boundary role at the epiploic foramen; the splenic vessels instead travel in the splenorenal ligament. The named folds are not interchangeable: each has a characteristic attachment and content, which is the most reliable way to identify it on cross-sectional imaging.

questions.chapterTitle: The anterior abdominal wall and peritoneum
questions.question: Which ligament forms the left lateral boundary of the lesser sac in continuity with the gastrosplenic ligament?
questions.explanation: Correct answer: C. The splenorenal ligament is continuous with the gastrosplenic ligament and contributes to the left lateral boundary of the lesser sac. It carries the splenic vessels between the pancreatic tail and splenic hilum. These spaces are potential compartments connected by defined routes rather than completely sealed cavities. Their boundaries and dependent positions help explain where fluid or infection may accumulate on CT or ultrasound.

questions.chapterTitle: The anterior abdominal wall and peritoneum
questions.question: What is the clinical significance of the peritoneal spaces and gutters on CT?

options.text: They are visible only on plain radiographs
They prevent all fluid movement between compartments
They help predict where fluid, pus or malignant disease may collect and spread

correctAnswer.text: They help predict where fluid, pus or malignant disease may collect and spread

questions.explanation: Correct answer: D. Peritoneal spaces are not isolated bags; their reflections and communicating channels guide movement of fluid. Knowledge of the subphrenic, subhepatic, paracolic and pelvic recesses helps radiologists describe collections and anticipate pathways of spread. These spaces are potential compartments connected by defined routes rather than completely sealed cavities. Their boundaries and dependent positions help explain where fluid or infection may accumulate on CT or ultrasound.

questions.chapterTitle: The anterior abdominal wall and peritoneum
questions.question: Which named space is situated inferior to the transverse mesocolon and contains much of the small bowel?
questions.explanation: Correct answer: A. The transverse mesocolon separates the supramesocolic region from the inframesocolic compartment. Much of the small bowel lies below this mesentery, and the right and left inframesocolic spaces are further described in relation to the small-bowel mesentery. These spaces are potential compartments connected by defined routes rather than completely sealed cavities. Their boundaries and dependent positions help explain where fluid or infection may accumulate on CT or ultrasound.

questions.chapterTitle: The anterior abdominal wall and peritoneum
questions.question: Which structure forms the anterior boundary of the lesser sac over much of its extent?
questions.explanation: Correct answer: D. The lesser sac is positioned behind the stomach and lesser omentum. Its posterior relation includes the pancreas and posterior abdominal structures, so it is a distinct potential space rather than part of the abdominal wall layers. These spaces are potential compartments connected by defined routes rather than completely sealed cavities. Their boundaries and dependent positions help explain where fluid or infection may accumulate on CT or ultrasound.

questions.chapterTitle: The anterior abdominal wall and peritoneum
questions.question: Which named fold connects the liver to the diaphragm and anterior abdominal wall?
questions.explanation: Correct answer: D. The falciform ligament attaches the anterosuperior liver to the anterior abdominal wall and diaphragm. It is an important surface landmark and continues inferiorly with the ligamentum teres fissure. The named folds are not interchangeable: each has a characteristic attachment and content, which is the most reliable way to identify it on cross-sectional imaging.

questions.chapterTitle: The anterior abdominal wall and peritoneum
questions.question: Which abdominal wall structure is a fibrous midline landmark on axial imaging?
questions.explanation: Correct answer: A. The linea alba is the midline raphe formed by interweaving aponeuroses. On axial imaging it separates the paired rectus abdominis muscles; the linea semilunaris instead marks the lateral border of rectus. On cross-sectional imaging, use the midline, rectus borders and fascial planes as landmarks; confusing a superficial fascial layer with a deep aponeurotic or peritoneal structure can mislocalize a lesion.

questions.question: Which imaging finding is characteristic of the arterial phase spleen compared with its portal venous phase appearance?

options.text: It has the same attenuation as air

questions.explanation: The chapter illustrates that the spleen can enhance heterogeneously during the arterial phase, including wedge-like or ring-like patterns. This is a normal perfusion phenomenon and should not automatically be mistaken for splenic pathology; the portal venous phase is more homogeneous.

questions.question: What is the approximate mass of the liver stated in the chapter?

options.text: About 5 kg in a typical adult

questions.explanation: The liver is described as the largest and heaviest solid organ, weighing approximately 1.5 kg. Its size and broad contact with surrounding structures make it a major landmark on abdominal cross-sectional imaging.

questions.question: How many Couinaud segments are described for the liver?

options.text: Six, one for each hepatic vein
Twelve, arranged by the portal triads
Four, corresponding only to the anatomical lobes

questions.explanation: The chapter describes nine segments in total: segment I is the caudate lobe, and segments II–VIII form the remaining eight functional segments. This is more useful for functional and surgical anatomy than the older division into right, left, quadrate and caudate lobes.

questions.question: Which Couinaud segment corresponds to the caudate lobe?
questions.explanation: The caudate lobe is segment I. It is anatomically distinctive because of its relationship to the inferior vena cava and its relatively independent vascular drainage, making it important to identify on axial and coronal imaging.

questions.question: Which vessels are used as landmarks to divide the liver into its functional segments?

options.text: Cystic duct and common bile duct

questions.explanation: The chapter uses portal and hepatic veins as the principal landmarks in segmental anatomy. Hepatic veins divide the liver into sections, while portal venous branches further divide these into superior and inferior segments.

questions.question: How do the three major hepatic veins divide the liver according to the chapter?

options.text: Into two equal anatomical lobes only
Into the caudate and quadrate lobes

questions.explanation: The right, middle and left hepatic veins divide the liver into four sections. The portal veins then subdivide these sections into superior and inferior segments, yielding the eight segments in addition to segment I.

questions.question: What is Riedel’s lobe?

options.text: A malignant mass arising from the caudate lobe
A congenital absence of the left hepatic lobe
A fold of peritoneum around the gallbladder
A normal inferior extension of the right hepatic lobe, often near segment VI

correctAnswer.text: A normal inferior extension of the right hepatic lobe, often near segment VI

questions.explanation: Riedel’s lobe is a normal variant in which the right hepatic lobe extends inferiorly, often around segment VI. On a plain film or cross-sectional study it may mimic hepatomegaly, so the shape should be interpreted in context rather than assumed to represent disease.

questions.question: Which peritoneal structure extends from the umbilicus to the liver and contains the ligamentum teres?
questions.explanation: The falciform ligament is a double fold of peritoneum extending between the anterior abdominal wall at the umbilicus and the liver. It contains the ligamentum teres, the fibrous remnant of the fetal umbilical vein.

questions.question: What is the ligamentum teres hepatis a remnant of?
questions.explanation: The ligamentum teres is the remnant of the umbilical vein, which carried oxygenated blood from the placenta toward the fetal liver and ductus venosus. In portal hypertension, this vein may recanalize and become visible as a collateral pathway.

questions.question: Where does the fetal umbilical vein connect within the liver as described in the chapter?

options.text: Directly to the right hepatic vein
To the splenic vein at the hilum

questions.explanation: The fetal umbilical vein connects with the left portal vein and directs oxygenated placental blood toward the ductus venosus and inferior vena cava. This relationship explains why the ligamentum teres lies in the falciform ligament and why the vessel can recanalize in portal hypertension.

questions.question: Which abnormal vascular finding may be seen in the falciform ligament in portal hypertension?

options.text: Dilatation of the cystic duct only

questions.explanation: The chapter notes that the umbilical vein can recanalize in portal hypertension. This creates a portosystemic collateral pathway along the falciform ligament and may be visible on contrast-enhanced CT as a prominent vessel.

questions.question: Which ligaments attach the liver to the diaphragm and define the bare area?

options.text: Round and broad ligaments of the uterus
Falciform ligament alone, without other reflections
Coronary ligaments, continuing as the right triangular ligament, and the left triangular ligament

correctAnswer.text: Coronary ligaments, continuing as the right triangular ligament, and the left triangular ligament

questions.explanation: The coronary peritoneal reflections attach the liver to the diaphragm and continue laterally as the triangular ligaments. The bare area lies between these reflections and lacks peritoneal covering, which is important when describing the liver’s posterior surface.

questions.question: What is the principal vascular feature of hepatic blood supply?

options.text: Supply only from the inferior vena cava
Supply exclusively from the hepatic veins
Dual supply from the portal vein and hepatic artery
Supply exclusively from the hepatic artery

correctAnswer.text: Dual supply from the portal vein and hepatic artery

questions.explanation: The liver has dual inflow: the portal vein supplies most of the blood volume, while the hepatic artery supplies the remainder. This distinction matters when interpreting enhancement phases and when considering the effects of vascular compromise.

questions.question: Approximately what proportion of hepatic blood supply is provided by the portal vein in the chapter?
questions.explanation: The chapter assigns approximately 85% of hepatic blood supply to the portal vein and 15% to the hepatic artery. The portal vein carries nutrient-rich venous blood from the gastrointestinal tract and spleen, while the hepatic artery provides oxygenated arterial blood.

questions.question: Approximately what proportion of hepatic blood supply is provided by the hepatic artery?
questions.explanation: The hepatic artery contributes approximately 15% of the liver’s blood supply according to the chapter. Although it contributes less volume than the portal vein, its arterial inflow is important for hepatic oxygen delivery and biliary structures.

questions.question: From which major artery does the common hepatic artery arise?

options.text: Superior mesenteric artery in every individual

questions.explanation: The usual common hepatic artery arises from the coeliac trunk. The chapter also emphasizes anatomical variants, including hepatic arterial branches arising from the superior mesenteric or left gastric arteries, so the expected pattern should not be assumed in every patient.

questions.question: Which branch is given off before the common hepatic artery becomes the hepatic artery proper?
questions.explanation: The common hepatic artery gives off branches including the right gastric artery and then the gastroduodenal artery near the epiploic foramen before continuing as the hepatic artery proper. Recognizing this sequence helps identify vessels around the pancreatic head and porta hepatis.

questions.question: Within the free edge of the lesser omentum, where is the hepatic artery relative to the portal vein and common bile duct?

options.text: Inferior to the pancreas and behind the aorta
Anterior to the portal vein and to the left of the common bile duct
Posterior to both the portal vein and common bile duct
Lateral to the spleen and renal vein

correctAnswer.text: Anterior to the portal vein and to the left of the common bile duct

questions.explanation: The hepatic artery runs in the free edge of the lesser omentum, anterior to the portal vein and to the left of the common bile duct. These relationships form part of the portal triad arrangement and are useful when identifying structures on axial CT or at the porta hepatis.

questions.question: Where does the hepatic artery divide into right and left branches?
questions.explanation: The hepatic artery proper divides into right and left branches at the porta hepatis. The right branch commonly supplies the right liver and gives rise to the cystic artery, although arterial variants can alter these relationships.

questions.question: What does the term “replaced hepatic artery” indicate in the chapter’s terminology?

options.text: An artery arising from an alternative source in the absence of the usual artery
A vein that has replaced the portal vein
A hepatic artery that has been surgically reconstructed
An extra artery present in addition to the usual artery

correctAnswer.text: An artery arising from an alternative source in the absence of the usual artery

questions.explanation: A replaced artery arises from an alternative origin and substitutes for the expected vessel, whereas an accessory artery is an additional vessel alongside the usual artery. This distinction is important for accurate vascular mapping before hepatobiliary surgery or intervention.

questions.question: Which artery is a common alternative source for a replaced right hepatic artery?
questions.explanation: The chapter notes that a replaced right hepatic artery may arise from the superior mesenteric artery. This variant changes the vessel’s course and is important to recognize during interpretation and surgical planning around the pancreatic head and porta hepatis.

questions.question: Which artery may give rise to a left hepatic artery variant?
questions.explanation: A left hepatic artery may arise from the left gastric artery as an accessory or replaced vessel. The chapter notes that these variants are relatively common, reinforcing the need to trace the arterial origin rather than identify vessels solely by expected position.

questions.question: Where is the portal vein formed?

options.text: By union of the inferior mesenteric and renal veins anterior to the liver
By union of the cystic and common bile ducts
By union of the splenic vein and superior mesenteric vein posterior to the pancreatic neck
By union of the hepatic veins at the diaphragm

correctAnswer.text: By union of the splenic vein and superior mesenteric vein posterior to the pancreatic neck

questions.explanation: The portal vein is formed by the splenic vein and superior mesenteric vein posterior to the neck of the pancreas, around the L1–L2 level. This location is a key landmark on axial CT and explains the close relationship of the portal confluence to the pancreas.

questions.question: What is the position of the portal vein relative to the hepatic artery and common bile duct in the free edge of the lesser omentum?

options.text: Always to the left of both

questions.explanation: Within the free edge of the lesser omentum, the portal vein lies posterior to the hepatic artery and common bile duct. This posterior position is a central part of the portal triad arrangement and helps distinguish the vein from the more anterior structures on cross-sectional images.

questions.question: Which venous pathways may enlarge as portosystemic collaterals in portal hypertension?

options.text: Oesophageal, umbilical and retroperitoneal venous channels

correctAnswer.text: Oesophageal, umbilical and retroperitoneal venous channels

questions.explanation: The chapter describes portosystemic anastomoses at the oesophagus, umbilicus and retroperitoneum. When portal pressure rises, these alternate venous routes can become prominent; oesophageal varices and a recanalized umbilical vein are important imaging manifestations.

questions.question: Why can oesophageal varices develop in portal hypertension?

options.text: The hepatic artery becomes the oesophagus’s only blood supply
Portal blood is diverted through portosystemic venous anastomoses
The common bile duct compresses the oesophageal lumen
The portal vein normally drains into the pulmonary veins

correctAnswer.text: Portal blood is diverted through portosystemic venous anastomoses

questions.explanation: Raised portal venous pressure encourages blood to flow through collateral connections between portal and systemic venous systems, including veins around the lower oesophagus. These dilated veins may appear as varices on CT and have clinical significance because they can bleed.

questions.question: Which imaging phase generally shows more homogeneous splenic enhancement and greater opacification of portal and systemic veins?
questions.explanation: The chapter contrasts arterial-phase images, in which the spleen may be heterogeneous and portal/systemic veins less opacified, with portal venous-phase images showing more homogeneous splenic enhancement and stronger venous opacification. Phase awareness helps avoid misreading normal enhancement patterns.

questions.question: What approximate maximum dimensions are given for the gallbladder?

options.text: 30 cm long and 15 cm in diameter
2 cm long and 1 mm in diameter
20 cm long and 10 cm in diameter
Up to 10 cm long and 3 cm in diameter

correctAnswer.text: Up to 10 cm long and 3 cm in diameter

questions.explanation: The chapter describes a pear-shaped gallbladder up to about 10 cm long and 3 cm in diameter. Size alone is not sufficient to diagnose disease; wall thickness, distension, stones and surrounding inflammatory change also matter on ultrasound and CT.

questions.question: What is the expected gallbladder wall thickness stated in the chapter?

options.text: The wall cannot be assessed on ultrasound
Less than 10 mm in every normal patient

questions.explanation: The chapter gives a normal gallbladder wall thickness of less than 4 mm. Wall thickening must be interpreted with the clinical context and degree of distension because it can occur in cholecystitis and in several systemic conditions.

questions.question: Where does the gallbladder hang from?

options.text: The posterior surface of the left kidney
The anterior surface of the pancreas
The inferior surface of the liver
The superior surface of the spleen

correctAnswer.text: The inferior surface of the liver

questions.explanation: The gallbladder lies against the inferior surface of the liver, with its fundus usually projecting anteriorly and inferiorly relative to the body and neck. This location helps identify it on ultrasound and axial imaging, particularly near the liver’s right lobe.

questions.question: What is Hartmann’s pouch?

options.text: A peritoneal recess behind the pancreas
A ventral dilatation near the gallbladder neck that may follow stone impaction
The normal fundus of every gallbladder
The distal end of the common bile duct

correctAnswer.text: A ventral dilatation near the gallbladder neck that may follow stone impaction

questions.explanation: Hartmann’s pouch is described as a ventral dilatation around the gallbladder neck that can occur after gallstone impaction; it is not presented as a normal feature in every gallbladder. It should be distinguished from the ordinary fundus and from the cystic duct.

questions.question: Which structure arises from the gallbladder neck and travels toward the porta hepatis?
questions.explanation: The cystic duct arises from the gallbladder neck and courses toward the porta hepatis, where it joins the hepatic ductal system. Understanding this route helps interpret biliary anatomy and locate the cystic duct during ultrasound, CT or cholangiographic studies.

questions.question: What is the spiral valve of Heister?

options.text: A normal calcified ring in the gallbladder wall
A fold inside the portal vein
Spiral mucosal folds in the gallbladder neck and cystic duct
A valve at the duodenal ileocaecal junction

correctAnswer.text: Spiral mucosal folds in the gallbladder neck and cystic duct

questions.explanation: The gallbladder neck and cystic duct contain spiral mucosal folds known as the valve of Heister, which help regulate bile flow. On ultrasound these folds can be echogenic and may mimic gallstones, so their tubular/linear morphology and continuity should be assessed.

questions.question: Which structure can be mistaken for gallstones because it appears highly echogenic on ultrasound?

options.text: The hepatic veins in all patients
Spiral folds of the valve of Heister

correctAnswer.text: Spiral folds of the valve of Heister

questions.explanation: The spiral folds of Heister can appear highly echogenic and may be mistaken for calculi. Stones typically create a discrete echogenic focus and often cast posterior acoustic shadowing, whereas mucosal folds follow the cystic duct’s internal contour.

questions.question: Which part of the gallbladder is consistently described as covered by peritoneum?

options.text: The common bile duct wall only
The entire hepatic attachment surface only

questions.explanation: The chapter notes that the gallbladder is covered by peritoneum over the fundus and inferior surface, while its hepatic surface is attached to the liver. Occasionally it hangs from its own mesentery, an anatomical variant relevant to its mobility.

questions.question: What is the primary imaging relevance of knowing the biliary segmental drainage pattern?

options.text: It predicts the course of the ureters
It determines the number of ribs on a radiograph
It replaces the need to identify the portal vein
It helps map which ducts drain individual liver segments

correctAnswer.text: It helps map which ducts drain individual liver segments

questions.explanation: Segmental biliary drainage maps the ducts serving different parts of the liver. This is important when interpreting cholangiography and cross-sectional imaging, and when planning surgery or intervention that may affect drainage from a specific segment.

questions.question: Which ductal structure is associated with the pancreatic head and joins the biliary pathway near the duodenum?

options.text: Cystic duct only, ending at the spleen

questions.explanation: The common bile duct descends toward the pancreatic head and the duodenum, where it joins the pancreatic ductal system in the usual arrangement. Its relationship to the pancreatic head is a key landmark on CT, MRI and ultrasound when evaluating obstructive biliary disease.

questions.question: Which part of the pancreas is closest to the splenic hilum?
questions.explanation: The pancreatic tail extends toward the splenic hilum and lies within the splenorenal ligament region. This close relationship matters when tracing the distal pancreas on CT and when considering splenic or pancreatic-tail disease.

questions.question: Which part of the pancreas lies posterior to the superior mesenteric vessels and projects around them?
questions.explanation: The uncinate process is a projection of the pancreatic head that extends posterior to the superior mesenteric vessels. This relationship is especially useful on axial CT because it helps distinguish the uncinate process from the head and nearby duodenum.

questions.question: Which embryological event gives rise to the annular pancreas described in the chapter?

options.text: Abnormal migration of the ventral pancreatic bud around the duodenum
Failure of the spleen to rotate
Failure of the kidneys to ascend

correctAnswer.text: Abnormal migration of the ventral pancreatic bud around the duodenum

questions.explanation: The chapter illustrates annular pancreas as a developmental anomaly related to abnormal migration of the ventral pancreatic bud, which can encircle the duodenum. Cross-sectional imaging may show pancreatic tissue around the duodenum, sometimes associated with narrowing or obstruction.

questions.question: What developmental mechanism causes pancreas divisum?

options.text: Failure of the gallbladder to form
Failure of fusion of the ventral and dorsal pancreatic duct systems
Failure of the hepatic veins to join the IVC
Persistence of the fetal umbilical arteries

correctAnswer.text: Failure of fusion of the ventral and dorsal pancreatic duct systems

questions.explanation: Pancreas divisum results when the dorsal and ventral pancreatic duct systems fail to fuse normally. The chapter highlights this as a ductal variant; recognizing the pattern on MRCP or other ductal imaging can explain an atypical drainage arrangement.

questions.question: Which imaging method is particularly suited to showing pancreatic ducts without ionizing radiation?
questions.explanation: MRCP uses heavily T2-weighted MRI techniques to display fluid-filled biliary and pancreatic ducts. It is useful for delineating ductal anatomy and variants such as pancreas divisum without requiring ionizing radiation.

questions.question: Which relationship is expected between the pancreas and lesser sac?

options.text: The lesser sac is inside the pancreatic duct
The pancreas lies anterior to the skin and superficial fascia
The pancreas forms an important posterior relation to the lesser sac
The pancreas is entirely within the gallbladder

correctAnswer.text: The pancreas forms an important posterior relation to the lesser sac

questions.explanation: The lesser sac lies posterior to the stomach and anterior to structures including the pancreas. This relationship explains why fluid associated with pancreatic inflammation can collect in the lesser sac and why its location is relevant on CT.

questions.question: Which vascular structure is closely related to the posterior aspect of the pancreatic neck where the portal vein forms?
questions.explanation: The portal vein is formed by the splenic vein and superior mesenteric vein posterior to the pancreatic neck. Because of this close relationship, the confluence should be assessed when evaluating pancreatic masses or inflammation that may affect the portal venous system.

questions.question: Which organ is shown on ultrasound as usually more echogenic than the kidney in the chapter’s illustration?
questions.explanation: The chapter’s ultrasound figure notes that the spleen is usually hyperechoic compared with the kidney. Echogenicity is a relative imaging descriptor and should be assessed alongside organ texture, size, vascularity and clinical context.

questions.question: Which surfaces are described for the spleen?
questions.explanation: The spleen has a diaphragmatic surface facing the diaphragm and a visceral surface related to neighbouring abdominal organs. These surfaces and the splenic hilum help orient the organ on axial CT and ultrasound.

questions.question: What is the significance of the splenic hilum on Doppler ultrasound?

options.text: It is the entry/exit region for splenic vessels
It is the site where the common bile duct enters the liver
It is the origin of the ureter

correctAnswer.text: It is the entry/exit region for splenic vessels

questions.explanation: The splenic vessels enter and leave at the splenic hilum, which can be demonstrated with colour Doppler. The hilum is also a useful landmark when tracing the splenic artery and vein and when evaluating focal lesions near the medial spleen.

questions.question: Why should heterogeneous splenic enhancement in the arterial phase be interpreted cautiously?

options.text: It is caused only by motion artefact
It can be a normal perfusion pattern

correctAnswer.text: It can be a normal perfusion pattern

questions.explanation: The chapter shows several normal arterial-phase splenic enhancement patterns, including wedge-like and ring-like appearances. Correlation with the phase of contrast administration and the portal venous images helps avoid overcalling normal perfusion heterogeneity as disease.

questions.question: Which structure lies between the left kidney and spleen region and is associated with the pancreatic tail?
questions.explanation: The splenorenal (lienorenal) ligament connects the spleen to the posterior abdominal wall region and contains the splenic vessels and pancreatic tail. This relationship explains why pathology near the pancreatic tail may extend toward the splenic hilum.

questions.question: At approximately which vertebral level does the coeliac trunk arise from the abdominal aorta in the chapter?
questions.explanation: The chapter’s aortic branch diagram places the coeliac trunk at approximately T12. Knowing the levels of major aortic branches helps orient sagittal and axial CT and distinguish the coeliac trunk from the superior mesenteric artery, which arises lower at about L1.

questions.question: At approximately which level does the superior mesenteric artery arise?
questions.explanation: The superior mesenteric artery is shown arising around L1, inferior to the coeliac trunk. Its origin is an important landmark on CT and its relationship to the pancreatic neck and third part of the duodenum is clinically significant.

questions.question: At approximately which level does the inferior mesenteric artery arise?
questions.explanation: The chapter locates the inferior mesenteric artery origin at approximately L3. This helps identify the vessel on sagittal and axial imaging and distinguish it from the superior mesenteric artery and the lower aortic bifurcation.

questions.question: At what approximate vertebral level does the abdominal aorta bifurcate?
questions.explanation: The aorta bifurcates into the common iliac arteries around L4 in the chapter’s diagram. This is a useful landmark on cross-sectional imaging and is distinct from the higher origins of the coeliac trunk and mesenteric arteries.

questions.question: Which vessels are the terminal branches of the abdominal aorta?

options.text: Right and left common iliac arteries

correctAnswer.text: Right and left common iliac arteries

questions.explanation: The abdominal aorta terminates by dividing into the common iliac arteries. These vessels then divide into internal and external iliac arteries, supplying the pelvis and lower limbs, respectively.

questions.question: Which artery is associated with the L1 level in the chapter’s aortic branch diagram?
questions.explanation: The superior mesenteric artery arises near L1, while the inferior mesenteric artery is lower around L3 and the aortic bifurcation is around L4. These level relationships help orient abdominal vascular anatomy on sagittal reconstructions.

questions.question: Which venous structure receives the hepatic veins before continuing to the right atrium?
questions.explanation: The hepatic veins drain directly into the inferior vena cava, which then passes through the diaphragm to the right atrium. This differs from the portal vein, which delivers blood to the liver and is not a direct systemic venous outflow vessel.

questions.question: Which description best distinguishes the portal vein from the inferior vena cava?

options.text: The portal vein carries blood to the liver, whereas the IVC returns systemic venous blood to the heart
The IVC carries blood from the bowel into the liver
Both are direct tributaries of the pulmonary artery
The portal vein drains the kidneys directly to the right atrium

correctAnswer.text: The portal vein carries blood to the liver, whereas the IVC returns systemic venous blood to the heart

questions.explanation: The portal vein brings blood from the gastrointestinal tract and spleen to the liver for processing, while the IVC returns systemic venous blood from the lower body to the heart. Their distinct functions and routes are fundamental when interpreting portal and systemic venous anatomy.

questions.question: Which venous channels may become prominent if the IVC is obstructed or absent?
questions.explanation: The chapter notes that the azygos and hemiazygos systems may continue from ascending lumbar or subcostal veins and can become more prominent when the IVC is blocked or absent. These channels provide an alternate route for blood to reach the superior vena cava.

questions.question: Where does the hemiazygos vein typically drain according to the chapter?

options.text: Into the portal vein at L1
Into the azygos vein around T9

correctAnswer.text: Into the azygos vein around T9

questions.explanation: The chapter describes the hemiazygos vein draining into the azygos vein at about T9. This cross-midline connection is part of the posterior thoracoabdominal venous network and may be important when collateral circulation is enlarged.

questions.question: Where does the azygos vein ultimately drain?
questions.explanation: The azygos vein arches over the root of the right lung and drains into the superior vena cava. Its connection with the ascending lumbar system can provide an important collateral pathway when normal IVC drainage is impaired.

questions.question: What is the cisterna chyli?

options.text: The terminal part of the common bile duct
The dilated proximal end of the thoracic duct
A peritoneal recess beside the spleen
The confluence of the hepatic veins

correctAnswer.text: The dilated proximal end of the thoracic duct

questions.explanation: The chapter identifies the cisterna chyli as the dilated proximal end of the thoracic duct, receiving lymph from abdominal lymphatic channels. It is a retroperitoneal structure and may be visible on cross-sectional imaging, particularly when enlarged or opacified.

questions.question: How are retroperitoneal lymph nodes commonly named in the chapter?

options.text: After the modality used to image them
Only by their distance from the umbilicus
By the number of bowel loops nearby

questions.explanation: Retroperitoneal nodes are named after adjacent anatomical structures, such as renal or para-aortic regions. Recognizing these regional names helps localize lymphadenopathy and communicate its distribution accurately in radiology reports.

questions.question: According to the chapter, where does abdominal lymph ultimately drain?

options.text: Into the cisterna chyli and then the thoracic duct

correctAnswer.text: Into the cisterna chyli and then the thoracic duct

questions.explanation: The chapter describes abdominal lymphatic drainage converging on the cisterna chyli, the dilated proximal end of the thoracic duct. This pathway ultimately returns lymph to the venous circulation, rather than joining the portal venous or biliary systems.

questions.question: Which modality is described as having a limited role for detailed anatomy of abdominal viscera and retroperitoneum?
questions.explanation: The chapter states that plain abdominal radiographs have a very limited role in evaluating detailed visceral and retroperitoneal anatomy. They may show organ outlines or calcification, but CT, MRI and ultrasound provide much better depiction of soft tissues and relationships.

questions.question: Which finding may occasionally be visible on a plain abdominal radiograph according to the chapter?

options.text: Calcification in structures such as the pancreas, spleen, adrenals, aorta, lymph nodes or gallbladder
All liver segments as separate outlines
The complete portal venous branching pattern
Normal pancreatic ducts in full detail

correctAnswer.text: Calcification in structures such as the pancreas, spleen, adrenals, aorta, lymph nodes or gallbladder

questions.explanation: Plain films may reveal calcification in the pancreas, spleen, adrenals, aorta, lymph nodes or gallbladder. They do not reliably depict the full soft-tissue anatomy or segmental vascular structures, so cross-sectional imaging is usually required for detailed assessment.

questions.question: Which modality can demonstrate the abdominal vessels using ultrasound imaging and Doppler?
questions.explanation: Ultrasound can show abdominal vessels in longitudinal and transverse planes, while Doppler assesses flow direction and vascularity. The chapter illustrates the aorta, IVC and coeliac artery, emphasizing the value of ultrasound for real-time vascular assessment.

questions.question: Which MRI signal relationship is listed for the spleen compared with the liver?

options.text: Higher on both T1 and T2
Lower on both T1 and T2
Equal signal on both sequences in all cases
Lower signal on T1-weighted images and higher signal on T2-weighted images

correctAnswer.text: Lower signal on T1-weighted images and higher signal on T2-weighted images

questions.explanation: The chapter’s table lists the spleen as lower in signal than liver on T1-weighted images and higher on T2-weighted images. These are relative signal descriptions, not absolute values, and sequence parameters and pathology can affect the observed appearance.

questions.question: Which MRI signal relationship is listed for the kidney compared with the liver?

options.text: Lower on T1-weighted images and higher on T2-weighted images
Higher on both T1 and T2
Lower on T1 and lower on T2 in every sequence
Equal on both T1 and T2

correctAnswer.text: Lower on T1-weighted images and higher on T2-weighted images

questions.explanation: In the chapter’s comparison table, the kidney has lower T1 signal and higher T2 signal than the liver. The comparison provides a broad reference for normal abdominal organ signal, though individual renal compartments and sequence settings alter the exact appearance.

questions.question: How is pancreatic signal described relative to liver on T1-weighted MRI in the chapter’s table?
questions.explanation: The chapter lists the pancreas as higher in T1 signal than the liver, attributing this to protein content, while its T2 signal is equal to or lower than liver. This is a comparative normal-organ reference rather than a substitute for assessing pancreatic texture and ductal anatomy.

questions.question: What is the key practical benefit of contrast phase awareness when reading abdominal CT?

options.text: It removes the need to know organ relationships
It allows CT to be interpreted without anatomy
It makes every organ enhance identically
It helps distinguish expected differences in arterial and venous enhancement of organs and vessels

correctAnswer.text: It helps distinguish expected differences in arterial and venous enhancement of organs and vessels

questions.explanation: Arterial and portal venous phases produce different patterns of enhancement in the liver, spleen and vascular structures. Knowing the phase prevents normal differences—such as heterogeneous arterial splenic enhancement or greater portal venous opacification—from being mistaken for pathology.

questions.question: Which organs are retroperitoneal landmarks commonly seen beside the aorta and IVC on upper abdominal CT?

options.text: The stomach and transverse colon only
The gallbladder and urinary bladder only

questions.explanation: The kidneys lie in the retroperitoneum on either side of the vertebral column, with the aorta and IVC forming central vascular landmarks. Their relationship to these vessels, the psoas muscles and the adrenal glands helps orient axial sections and localize retroperitoneal lesions.

questions.question: Where are the adrenal glands located in relation to the kidneys?

options.text: At the superomedial aspects of the kidneys

correctAnswer.text: At the superomedial aspects of the kidneys

questions.explanation: The adrenal glands sit near the superomedial poles of the kidneys and are separate from the renal parenchyma. On CT they are identified by their limbs and their relationship to the diaphragmatic crura, aorta, IVC and upper renal poles.

questions.question: Which major artery normally supplies the kidneys directly from the abdominal aorta?
questions.explanation: The renal arteries arise from the abdominal aorta and enter the renal hila. Their origins and branching pattern should be traced on arterial-phase CT because accessory or variant renal arteries can be present and may matter in intervention or surgery.

questions.question: Which vein typically crosses anterior to the aorta to reach the IVC?
questions.explanation: The left renal vein crosses anterior to the aorta to drain into the IVC, whereas the right renal vein is shorter and drains directly from the right kidney. This difference is a useful landmark when interpreting axial CT and assessing renal vascular relationships.

questions.question: Which structure is usually positioned to the right of the abdominal aorta?

options.text: Portal vein throughout its entire course

questions.explanation: In the abdomen, the IVC generally lies to the right of the aorta. This relationship provides a reliable orientation point on axial CT, although the vessels’ positions and appearances should be assessed at the level being examined.

questions.question: Which vessel is generally located to the left of the IVC and posterior to the pancreatic neck near its formation?
questions.explanation: The portal venous confluence forms posterior to the pancreatic neck and then ascends toward the liver. Its relationship to the aorta and IVC varies with the slice level, so the vein is best followed through contiguous images rather than identified from one cross-section alone.

questions.question: What is the principal role of the hepatic veins?

options.text: Drain blood from the liver into the IVC
Carry blood from the bowel to the liver
Supply arterial blood to the gallbladder

correctAnswer.text: Drain blood from the liver into the IVC

questions.explanation: The hepatic veins carry blood away from the liver and empty into the IVC. They should not be confused with portal venous branches, which carry blood into the liver and are used with hepatic veins to understand segmental anatomy.

questions.question: Which statement best describes the relationship between the hepatic veins and portal veins in liver segmentation?

options.text: Hepatic veins divide the liver into sections, and portal veins subdivide these into segments
Portal veins divide the liver into sections while hepatic veins form the portal triad
