Neither system is useful for segmental anatomy
Both systems drain directly into the common bile duct

correctAnswer.text: Hepatic veins divide the liver into sections, and portal veins subdivide these into segments

questions.explanation: The chapter describes the three hepatic veins as dividing the liver into four sections, with portal venous branches dividing these into superior and inferior segments. This vascular framework is central to Couinaud segmentation and supports precise localization of lesions.

questions.question: Which vessel lies in the free edge of the lesser omentum alongside the hepatic artery and portal vein?
questions.explanation: The hepatoduodenal ligament, the free edge of the lesser omentum, contains the portal triad: portal vein, hepatic artery and bile duct. Their relative positions are clinically useful, but arterial and ductal variants mean each structure should be traced rather than assumed from position alone.

questions.question: What is the usual relationship of the right hepatic artery to the portal vein noted in the chapter?

options.text: It passes anterior to the portal vein in about 90% of individuals
It always passes posterior to the portal vein
It always passes through the portal vein
It is absent in all normal individuals

correctAnswer.text: It passes anterior to the portal vein in about 90% of individuals

questions.explanation: The chapter notes that in about 90% of individuals the right hepatic artery passes anterior to the portal vein. A minority have a different relationship, illustrating why vascular anatomy should be verified on the patient’s own images before procedures.

questions.question: Which artery can give rise to the gastroduodenal artery before continuing as the hepatic artery proper?

options.text: Superior mesenteric artery in every case

questions.explanation: The common hepatic artery courses near the pancreatic head and gives off the gastroduodenal artery before continuing as the hepatic artery proper. This course is an important orientation feature on arterial-phase CT and angiography.

questions.question: What is the principal significance of accessory versus replaced hepatic arteries on imaging?

options.text: They prevent the liver from having portal venous supply
They indicate that the portal vein is absent
They alter the expected number or origin of arterial supplies to the liver
They are always evidence of trauma

correctAnswer.text: They alter the expected number or origin of arterial supplies to the liver

questions.explanation: An accessory artery adds an arterial supply, whereas a replaced artery arises from an alternative source in place of the usual vessel. These variants may change the risk profile of surgery or embolization, so arterial-phase imaging should map the origins and courses carefully.

questions.question: Which structure forms the anterior boundary of the lesser sac?
questions.explanation: The lesser sac lies behind the stomach and lesser omentum, with the pancreas forming an important posterior relation. This arrangement helps explain why upper abdominal fluid collections may occupy the lesser sac and why it is important to assess this space on CT.

questions.question: Which structure is the key posterior relation of the stomach in the lesser sac region?
questions.explanation: The pancreas lies posterior to the stomach across the lesser sac. This relationship is particularly important when pancreatic inflammation or a collection displaces the stomach or extends into the omental bursa.

questions.question: Which organ lies immediately beneath the left hemidiaphragm and has a diaphragmatic surface?
questions.explanation: The spleen lies in the left upper quadrant beneath the diaphragm and has a diaphragmatic surface. Its position relative to the left kidney, stomach and pancreatic tail provides useful landmarks on axial CT and ultrasound.

questions.question: Which structure is most directly related to the splenic hilum and pancreatic tail?
questions.explanation: The splenic artery and vein pass toward the splenic hilum, and the pancreatic tail extends toward this region. This close anatomical relationship is important when evaluating the distal pancreas, splenic vessels and adjacent collections.

questions.question: What does a normal Riedel’s lobe most directly risk being mistaken for on imaging?
questions.explanation: Riedel’s lobe is an inferior tongue-like extension of the right hepatic lobe and may make the liver appear elongated. The chapter identifies it as a normal variant, so recognition prevents an anatomical shape variant from being interpreted as pathological enlargement by itself.

questions.question: Which structure is the fibrous remnant of the fetal ductus venosus?
questions.explanation: The ligamentum venosum is the remnant of the fetal ductus venosus, while the ligamentum teres is the remnant of the umbilical vein. Distinguishing these structures helps orient the left liver and caudate region on anatomical images.

questions.question: Which fetal vessel carried oxygenated blood from the umbilical cord toward the liver?
questions.explanation: The fetal umbilical vein carried oxygenated blood from the placenta and connected with the left portal vein; some blood then passed through the ductus venosus toward the IVC. Its postnatal remnant is the ligamentum teres within the falciform ligament.

questions.question: Which imaging observation supports identifying the portal venous rather than early arterial phase?

options.text: Portal veins are unopacified and the spleen is maximally heterogeneous
All arteries and veins are completely invisible
More conspicuous portal and systemic veins with a more homogeneous spleen

correctAnswer.text: More conspicuous portal and systemic veins with a more homogeneous spleen

questions.explanation: On portal venous phase CT, the portal and systemic veins are more opacified and splenic enhancement is generally more homogeneous than in the arterial phase. Recognizing the phase is essential before interpreting organ enhancement as abnormal.

questions.question: What is the principal imaging limitation of a plain abdominal radiograph for the retroperitoneum?

options.text: It always shows all retroperitoneal nodes clearly
It provides better soft-tissue contrast than MRI
It provides little detail of soft-tissue organs and their relationships

correctAnswer.text: It provides little detail of soft-tissue organs and their relationships

questions.explanation: Plain radiographs can show selected organ outlines or calcifications, but they do not delineate retroperitoneal soft tissues and vascular relationships well. CT and MRI provide cross-sectional detail, while ultrasound is useful for focused evaluation and vascular Doppler.

questions.question: Which organ is often used as a reference for relative T1 and T2 signal intensity of other abdominal viscera in the chapter?
questions.explanation: The chapter’s table compares abdominal viscera with the liver on T1- and T2-weighted MRI. These relative signal descriptions offer a baseline for recognizing normal organ appearances, but should be applied with awareness of sequence parameters and tissue-specific variation.

questions.question: What is the listed T2-weighted MRI signal of muscle relative to liver?
questions.explanation: The chapter’s comparison table lists muscle as lower in signal than liver on both T1- and T2-weighted images. This is a general relative comparison and helps orient normal abdominal anatomy, though sequence settings and pathology can affect appearance.

questions.question: How is adrenal signal intensity compared with liver in the chapter’s MRI table?

options.text: Lower on T1 and always much higher on T2
Higher than liver on both sequences in all cases
Equal to or lower than liver on both T1- and T2-weighted images

correctAnswer.text: Equal to or lower than liver on both T1- and T2-weighted images

questions.explanation: The chapter lists the adrenal gland as equal to or lower in signal than liver on T1- and T2-weighted MRI. This provides a broad normal reference, but the gland’s small size and surrounding fat often make its shape and location more useful than signal alone for identification.

questions.question: What is the role of the coeliac trunk in abdominal arterial anatomy?

options.text: It is the terminal branch of the IVC
It supplies only the lower limb
It is a major anterior branch of the aorta supplying foregut-related structures
It drains the liver into the portal vein

correctAnswer.text: It is a major anterior branch of the aorta supplying foregut-related structures

questions.explanation: The coeliac trunk arises from the upper abdominal aorta and gives rise to major branches including the left gastric, splenic and common hepatic arteries. Its origin near T12 is an important landmark when following the upper abdominal arterial tree.

questions.question: Which major branch of the abdominal aorta supplies much of the midgut?
questions.explanation: The superior mesenteric artery arises around L1 and supplies much of the midgut. In imaging, its origin and its relationship to the pancreatic neck and third part of the duodenum are key landmarks for evaluating the mesenteric root and adjacent anatomy.

questions.question: Which major branch of the abdominal aorta supplies hindgut structures?
questions.explanation: The inferior mesenteric artery arises around L3 and supplies hindgut structures. Its lower origin distinguishes it from the coeliac trunk and superior mesenteric artery on sagittal vascular reconstructions.

questions.question: Which vessel is the principal arterial supply to the spleen?
questions.explanation: The splenic artery arises from the coeliac trunk and courses toward the splenic hilum, closely related to the pancreas. Tracing its course is useful on arterial-phase CT and when assessing vascular anatomy around the pancreatic tail and spleen.

questions.question: Which vessel accompanies the splenic artery toward the splenic hilum but returns blood from the spleen?
questions.explanation: The splenic vein drains the spleen and courses toward the portal venous confluence, where it joins the superior mesenteric vein behind the pancreatic neck. It often lies posterior to the pancreas and is a useful landmark when assessing pancreatic pathology.

questions.question: Why is the portal venous confluence a useful landmark in pancreatic imaging?

options.text: It lies posterior to the pancreatic neck and is formed by the splenic and superior mesenteric veins
It is the terminal drainage of the hepatic veins
It lies within the gallbladder fundus

correctAnswer.text: It lies posterior to the pancreatic neck and is formed by the splenic and superior mesenteric veins

questions.explanation: The portal venous confluence lies immediately posterior to the pancreatic neck and is formed by the splenic and superior mesenteric veins. Its relationship to the pancreas makes it important when evaluating pancreatic masses, inflammation or venous involvement.

questions.question: Which structures are assigned to the foregut in the chapter?

options.text: The pharynx, oesophagus, stomach and first two parts of the duodenum
The caecum, appendix and entire colon
The jejunum, ileum and ascending colon
The distal transverse colon through the rectum only

correctAnswer.text: The pharynx, oesophagus, stomach and first two parts of the duodenum

questions.explanation: The chapter groups the pharynx, oesophagus, stomach and first and second parts of the duodenum as foregut derivatives. This embryological grouping is clinically useful because it corresponds broadly to coeliac arterial supply, while the more distal bowel is supplied predominantly by the superior or inferior mesenteric arteries.

questions.question: Which major artery predominantly supplies the foregut derivatives described in the chapter?
questions.explanation: The chapter identifies the coeliac artery as the principal arterial supply for foregut structures. There are stated exceptions along the oesophagus: the middle oesophagus receives direct branches from the thoracic aorta and the proximal third from inferior thyroid vessels, so the broad embryological rule should not be applied without considering the level.

questions.question: Which structures form the midgut according to the chapter?

options.text: The third and fourth parts of the duodenum through the proximal two-thirds of the transverse colon
The pharynx through the second part of the duodenum
The distal third of the transverse colon, descending colon and rectum

correctAnswer.text: The third and fourth parts of the duodenum through the proximal two-thirds of the transverse colon

questions.explanation: The midgut includes the third and fourth duodenal parts, jejunum, ileum, caecum, appendix, ascending colon and proximal two-thirds of the transverse colon. This grouping aligns with predominant supply from the superior mesenteric artery and helps explain the vascular territories of bowel disease.

questions.question: Which artery predominantly supplies the midgut?
questions.explanation: The superior mesenteric artery and its branches supply the midgut territory. This includes much of the small bowel and the right colon, with the chapter defining the proximal two-thirds of the transverse colon as midgut rather than hindgut.

questions.question: Which bowel segments are described as hindgut derivatives?

options.text: The jejunum, ileum and ascending colon
The distal transverse colon, descending colon, sigmoid colon, rectum and anus

correctAnswer.text: The distal transverse colon, descending colon, sigmoid colon, rectum and anus

questions.explanation: The hindgut forms the distal transverse colon, descending and sigmoid colon, rectum and anus. Its predominant arterial supply is the inferior mesenteric artery, although the rectum also receives supply from internal iliac branches; this is a useful reminder that rectal vascular anatomy is not exclusively mesenteric.

questions.question: What is the predominant arterial supply of the hindgut?
questions.explanation: The inferior mesenteric artery supplies most hindgut derivatives, including the distal transverse and descending colon and sigmoid colon. The rectum has additional arterial supply from internal iliac branches, which is relevant when tracing pelvic vascular anatomy.

questions.question: At approximately what gestational age does the midgut begin to herniate into the umbilical cord in the chapter?
questions.explanation: The chapter states that the midgut herniates into the umbilical cord at about 5 weeks and returns to the abdominal cavity at about 10 weeks. These developmental movements establish the normal relative positions of the small bowel and proximal colon.

questions.question: How much anticlockwise rotation of the midgut is described as it returns to the abdomen?
questions.explanation: The chapter describes a 270-degree anticlockwise rotation during return of the midgut to the abdomen. This rotation places the fourth part of the duodenum and jejunum to the left of the midline and the proximal colon to the right; abnormal rotation can produce malposition and a narrow mesenteric base.

questions.question: What arrangement is described in midgut malrotation?

options.text: The rectum rotates anterior to the bladder
The entire colon lies in the pelvis and the stomach in the right lower quadrant
The duodenojejunal flexure and jejunum may remain on the right, with colon on the left
The stomach and spleen exchange positions

correctAnswer.text: The duodenojejunal flexure and jejunum may remain on the right, with colon on the left

questions.explanation: With malrotation, the chapter notes that the duodenojejunal flexure and jejunum may remain on the right and the colon on the left. The small-bowel mesentery is short and vulnerable to twisting, which can cause volvulus, obstruction and ischaemia; the position of bowel alone should prompt assessment of the mesenteric arrangement.

questions.question: What is the principal risk associated with the short mesentery in midgut malrotation?

options.text: Isolated gastric outlet obstruction from a hypertrophied pylorus in every case
Twisting with volvulus, obstruction and possible ischaemia

correctAnswer.text: Twisting with volvulus, obstruction and possible ischaemia

questions.explanation: The chapter links the short mesentery in malrotation to twisting (volvulus), with potential duodenal obstruction and bowel ischaemia. The concern is not simply an unusual bowel position: the altered mesenteric base creates a mechanical risk to intestinal perfusion.

questions.question: What does the chapter call failure of the midgut to return into the abdominal cavity?
questions.explanation: The chapter calls failure of the midgut to return to the abdomen exomphalos, with small and large bowel herniating through the abdominal wall at birth. This is distinct from malrotation, in which the bowel returns but rotates abnormally.

questions.question: At which vertebral level does the pharynx connect to the cervical oesophagus?
questions.explanation: The pharynx extends from the base of the skull to approximately C6, where it continues as the cervical oesophagus. This level is a useful cross-sectional landmark when distinguishing the lower pharynx from the oesophagus on sagittal MRI or CT.

questions.question: Which structure protects the larynx during swallowing, as described in the pharyngeal anatomy section?
questions.explanation: The epiglottis helps protect the laryngeal inlet during swallowing. On imaging, its position and the adjacent valleculae and piriform fossae help orient the hypopharynx; these structures should be recognized as related but distinct spaces.

questions.question: Which paired recesses are formed posterolaterally as the laryngopharynx drapes around the larynx?

options.text: The pyriform recesses of the stomach

questions.explanation: The piriform fossae are posterolateral recesses of the laryngopharynx beside the larynx. They are visible on cross-sectional and contrast studies and are important landmarks for the passage of swallowed material toward the cervical oesophagus.

questions.question: Which structure forms the superior boundary of the pharyngeal space described in the chapter?
questions.explanation: The chapter describes the soft palate as the superior boundary and the epiglottis as the inferior boundary of the pharyngeal region under discussion. The anterior relationship is to the base of tongue and epiglottis, while prevertebral muscles lie posterior to the oropharynx.

questions.question: Which structures lie posterior to the oropharynx?
questions.explanation: The prevertebral muscles lie posterior to the oropharynx. This relationship provides a useful orientation landmark on axial neck imaging, where the pharyngeal lumen is anterior to the prevertebral muscular plane.

questions.question: Which sequence best describes the wall layers illustrated for the oesophagus?

options.text: Mucosa, submucosa, muscularis propria and outer adventitia, with mucosal subdivisions visible on imaging

correctAnswer.text: Mucosa, submucosa, muscularis propria and outer adventitia, with mucosal subdivisions visible on imaging

questions.explanation: The chapter illustrates the oesophageal wall with mucosal layers, submucosa, muscularis propria and adventitia. Unlike much of the intraperitoneal bowel, the oesophagus does not have a continuous outer serosal covering; recognizing the wall layers helps interpret contrast studies and cross-sectional appearances.

questions.question: Why is the oesophagus often identifiable on chest imaging even when its lumen is not distended?

options.text: Because it has a calcified wall in normal adults
By its relationships and impressions from adjacent mediastinal structures
Because it is surrounded by bone
Because it always contains a large gas bubble

correctAnswer.text: By its relationships and impressions from adjacent mediastinal structures

questions.explanation: The oesophagus is assessed in relation to adjacent structures such as the aortic arch, left main bronchus, left atrium and descending aorta, which create recognizable impressions on contrast studies. Its visibility therefore depends on both the lumen and the surrounding mediastinal anatomy, not on constant gas filling.

questions.question: Which adjacent structures produce normal impressions on the thoracic oesophagus in a barium study?

options.text: The right kidney, caecum and appendix
The gallbladder and common bile duct
The aortic arch, left main bronchus and left atrium

correctAnswer.text: The aortic arch, left main bronchus and left atrium

questions.explanation: The chapter depicts impressions from the aortic arch, left main bronchus and left atrium on the thoracic oesophagus. These normal external impressions help localize the oesophagus in a barium swallow and should be distinguished from intrinsic narrowing or a mucosal lesion.

questions.question: Which major vessel lies posterior to the thoracic oesophagus in its lower course and may create an impression?
questions.explanation: The descending aorta is an important posterior relation of the thoracic oesophagus and can produce a visible impression. The exact relationships change along the oesophageal course, so interpretation benefits from correlating the level of an impression with cross-sectional anatomy.

questions.question: Which imaging methods does the chapter emphasize for viewing the GI tract in its entirety?
questions.explanation: The introduction emphasizes CT and MRI for imaging the small and large bowel in their entirety. Ultrasound is presented as a more focused tool for selected indications such as pyloric stenosis, appendicitis, terminal ileal disease and paediatric intussusception.

questions.question: At what approximate adult maximum volume is the stomach described in the chapter?
questions.explanation: The chapter gives an adult maximum stomach volume of approximately 1500 mL. This is a contextual anatomical figure rather than a fixed functional capacity; stomach shape and visibility on plain radiographs also vary with filling and patient position.

questions.question: Which arterial branch is associated with the lesser curve and gastro-oesophageal junction?
questions.explanation: The chapter associates the left gastric artery with the lesser curve and gastro-oesophageal junction. It notes that the vessel arises from the coeliac trunk, while the detailed arterial pattern around the stomach includes additional branches along the greater curve and pyloric region.

questions.question: Which artery supplies the greater curve through the right gastroepiploic branch?
questions.explanation: The right gastroepiploic artery arises from the gastroduodenal artery and supplies the greater curve. This helps distinguish the arterial supply of the greater curve from the left gastric supply along the lesser curve and gastro-oesophageal junction.

questions.question: Which structures form the two main curvatures of the stomach?

options.text: The lesser curve medially and the greater curve laterally/inferiorly
The proximal and distal ends of the oesophagus
The superior and inferior borders of the pancreas
The anterior and posterior walls of the rectum

correctAnswer.text: The lesser curve medially and the greater curve laterally/inferiorly

questions.explanation: The lesser and greater curves are the principal external contours used to orient the stomach on barium studies and CT. Gastric regions such as fundus, body, antrum and pylorus are described relative to these curves and to the gastro-oesophageal junction and duodenal cap.

questions.question: What are gastric rugae?

options.text: Valves within the common bile duct
Folds of the gastric mucosa visible when the stomach is not fully distended

correctAnswer.text: Folds of the gastric mucosa visible when the stomach is not fully distended

questions.explanation: Gastric rugae are mucosal folds and can be seen on contrast studies, particularly when the stomach is not fully distended. They should not be confused with the fixed contour of the gastric wall; adequate distension improves assessment of the lumen and mucosal outline.

questions.question: Why may the stomach not be visible on a plain abdominal radiograph?

options.text: The stomach is radiolucent only because of calcification
The stomach is normally outside the abdomen
It may be fluid-filled rather than containing gas
It is always hidden behind the pelvis

correctAnswer.text: It may be fluid-filled rather than containing gas

questions.explanation: The chapter notes that a fluid-filled stomach may not be conspicuous on a plain film. A gastric gas bubble is common but not obligatory, so absence of a visible bubble does not by itself imply abnormal position or absence of the stomach.

questions.question: Which stomach region is directly continuous with the duodenal cap?
questions.explanation: The pylorus forms the gastric outlet and is continuous with the duodenal cap, or first part of the duodenum. On a barium meal, the cap is a recognizable landmark immediately beyond the pyloric channel and should be differentiated from the more distal duodenal segments.

questions.question: Which parts of the duodenum are classified as foregut in the chapter?

options.text: The third and fourth parts only

questions.explanation: The first and second parts of the duodenum are included in the foregut, while the third and fourth parts are included in the midgut. The transition is important for embryological and vascular reasoning and illustrates that the duodenum spans two developmental territories.

questions.question: Which part of the duodenum is most closely related to the head of the pancreas and common bile duct?

options.text: The fourth part at the duodenojejunal flexure

questions.explanation: The second part of the duodenum descends alongside the pancreatic head and receives the common bile duct and pancreatic duct at the ampullary region. These intimate relationships explain why pancreatic and biliary pathology can affect the duodenal wall and vice versa.

questions.question: Which duodenal segment is crossed or indented by the superior mesenteric vessels and lies anterior to the aorta?
questions.explanation: The third part passes horizontally across the abdomen anterior to the aorta and is related to the superior mesenteric artery and vein. The chapter notes that these structures can indent it; the relationship is important when considering compression or obstruction at this level.

questions.question: Which position is characteristic of the duodenojejunal flexure in normal anatomy?

options.text: Inside the pelvis behind the rectum
Left of the midline near the level of L2
Right of the midline below the caecum

correctAnswer.text: Left of the midline near the level of L2

questions.explanation: The chapter places the duodenojejunal flexure at about L2 and to the left of the midline. It is a key landmark for distinguishing duodenum from jejunum and for recognizing abnormal positioning in malrotation.

questions.question: Which projection is described as best demonstrating the first part of the duodenum on a barium study?
questions.explanation: Because the first duodenal part has an oblique course, the chapter notes that it is best seen in the right anterior oblique projection. This positioning helps profile the duodenal cap and reduces superimposition that can obscure its contour.

questions.question: Where do the valvulae conniventes begin according to the chapter?

options.text: In the second part of the duodenum

correctAnswer.text: In the second part of the duodenum

questions.explanation: The chapter states that valvulae conniventes begin in the second part of the duodenum and become more conspicuous distally in the small bowel. These transverse mucosal folds help distinguish small bowel from the colon, whose haustra are generally more widely spaced and do not cross the entire lumen in the same way.

questions.question: Which venous structure drains the first 2.5 cm of the duodenum as described?
questions.explanation: The chapter states that the first 2.5 cm of the duodenum drains to the prepyloric vein. This short proximal segment has distinctive vascular and lymphatic relationships compared with the more distal duodenum, reflecting its position near the pylorus.

questions.question: Which lymph-node group receives drainage from the first 2.5 cm of the duodenum in the chapter?

options.text: The para-aortic nodes only, with no coeliac drainage

questions.explanation: The proximal 2.5 cm of the duodenum is described as draining to the coeliac lymph-node group. This localized pattern is relevant to understanding the spread of disease near the pylorus and should be distinguished from lymphatic pathways of the distal small bowel.

questions.question: Which artery is described as supplying the first part of the duodenum along with the right gastric and right gastroepiploic vessels?
questions.explanation: The chapter describes the gastroduodenal artery as contributing to supply of the first part of the duodenum, alongside the right gastric and right gastroepiploic arteries. The proximal duodenum has an arterial arrangement related to the stomach and pancreatic head, while more distal portions receive supply from superior mesenteric branches.

questions.question: At approximately which vertebral level is the duodenojejunal flexure located in the chapter?
questions.explanation: The chapter places the duodenojejunal flexure at approximately L2 and to the left of the midline. This landmark marks the transition from the fixed duodenum to the mobile jejunum and is useful when assessing bowel position; a right-sided flexure can raise concern for malrotation in the appropriate context.

questions.question: Which small-bowel segment typically has more prominent valvulae conniventes on contrast imaging?
questions.explanation: The jejunum typically shows prominent, closely spaced valvulae conniventes, which can give the bowel a feathery appearance on contrast studies. Fold prominence generally decreases toward the ileum, so fold pattern can help distinguish jejunal from ileal loops when interpreted with position and other landmarks.

questions.question: Which finding best supports identifying a loop as small bowel rather than colon on a contrast study?

options.text: Haustra that never cross the lumen
Valvulae conniventes that cross the lumen
The presence of a gastric ruga
A fixed haustral pattern in the rectum

correctAnswer.text: Valvulae conniventes that cross the lumen

questions.explanation: Valvulae conniventes are transverse folds that can cross the small-bowel lumen. Colonic haustra are different in configuration and typically do not extend across the entire lumen, making fold morphology a useful distinction on contrast studies and plain films.

questions.question: What is the purpose of adequate small-bowel distension during CT or MR enterography?

options.text: It intentionally collapses the lumen to obscure the mucosa
It prevents visualization of the mesentery
It thins the bowel wall and separates loops to improve assessment
It replaces the need for contrast in all examinations

correctAnswer.text: It thins the bowel wall and separates loops to improve assessment

questions.explanation: The chapter emphasizes adequate distension using an osmotic oral agent. Distension thins the wall and separates adjacent loops, improving evaluation of mural thickening, luminal narrowing and surrounding mesentery; collapsed loops can mimic thickening and reduce diagnostic confidence.

questions.question: What distinguishes CT enteroclysis from routine oral enterography in the chapter?

options.text: The colon is filled through a rectal catheter only
Contrast is injected directly into the hepatic artery
An oral contrast agent is pumped through a nasojejunal tube

correctAnswer.text: An oral contrast agent is pumped through a nasojejunal tube

questions.explanation: The chapter describes CT enteroclysis as using a nasojejunal tube to pump an oral agent into the small bowel. Controlled delivery can improve distension, but it is more invasive than drinking an oral contrast preparation and is used for selected diagnostic questions.

questions.question: For which clinical use does the chapter particularly describe MR enterography?

options.text: Initial diagnosis and follow-up of small-bowel disease such as Crohn’s disease
Primary imaging of the coronary arteries
Routine assessment of the skull base

correctAnswer.text: Initial diagnosis and follow-up of small-bowel disease such as Crohn’s disease

questions.explanation: The chapter notes that MR enterography is used mainly for initial diagnosis and follow-up, particularly for small-bowel inflammatory disease. It evaluates the bowel wall and extra-enteric tissues without ionizing radiation, which is useful when repeated imaging is anticipated.

questions.question: Which modality is described as a focused tool for evaluating the appendix and terminal ileum?
questions.explanation: High-frequency transabdominal ultrasound is described for focused assessment of the appendix and terminal ileum, including appendicitis and Crohn’s disease. It is not presented as replacing CT or MRI for complete evaluation of the entire bowel; its utility depends on the clinical question and visibility of the target segment.

questions.question: Which paediatric gastrointestinal condition is specifically listed as an ultrasound indication?

options.text: Colonic diverticulosis in all elderly patients

questions.explanation: The chapter lists ultrasound assessment of small and large bowel for intussusception in children. The modality can demonstrate bowel-within-bowel configuration, while CT and MRI have broader roles for whole-bowel assessment and selected complex cases.

questions.question: What is the main role of endocavity ultrasound in the lower GI tract described in the chapter?

options.text: Assessing the anal canal for sphincter tears and fistulae

correctAnswer.text: Assessing the anal canal for sphincter tears and fistulae

questions.explanation: The chapter describes endocavity ultrasound for visualization of the anal canal, including sphincter tears and fistulae. This focused approach provides high-resolution local anatomy and complements MRI when broader pelvic or fistula mapping is needed.

questions.question: What is a key advantage of cross-sectional imaging for GI anatomy emphasized in the introduction?

options.text: It shows the bowel’s relationships with adjacent abdominal structures and pathways of disease spread
It cannot show the entire bowel
It is useful only for measuring gastric acidity
It displays only the mucosal surface and no surrounding anatomy

correctAnswer.text: It shows the bowel’s relationships with adjacent abdominal structures and pathways of disease spread

questions.explanation: CT and MRI show the GI tract in relation to adjacent organs, vessels, mesentery and spaces. This helps localize disease and understand local or distant spread, which is one of the central reasons the chapter emphasizes cross-sectional anatomy rather than luminal studies alone.

questions.question: Where does the appendix arise from the caecum?

options.text: The greater curve of the stomach
The posteromedial wall of the caecum
The anterior wall of the rectum
The lateral wall of the descending colon

correctAnswer.text: The posteromedial wall of the caecum

questions.explanation: The appendix arises from the posteromedial wall of the caecum. Its base is therefore located by identifying the caecum and converging colonic taeniae where visible; the distal tip is mobile and can occupy several positions, so the base is often the more dependable landmark on CT or ultrasound.

questions.question: What proportion of appendices are described as retrocaecal in the chapter?
questions.explanation: The chapter states that the appendix is very mobile and is retrocaecal in approximately 75% of cases. This common position explains why the appendix may be difficult to visualize directly on ultrasound and why inflammation may present with atypical symptoms depending on the location of its tip.

questions.question: Which feature of the appendix mesentery is noted in the chapter?

options.text: It is attached directly to the liver by the falciform ligament
It often has its own, potentially long, mesentery containing its vessels
It lies inside the pancreatic duct
It has no blood supply and no mesentery

correctAnswer.text: It often has its own, potentially long, mesentery containing its vessels

questions.explanation: The appendix has its own mesentery, which may be long and contains its vessels. The length and mobility of the mesentery contribute to variable appendiceal position; on imaging, a tubular structure should be traced back to the caecal base rather than diagnosed solely by its apparent location.

questions.question: How does the appendiceal lumen change with age according to the chapter?

options.text: It is replaced by a vascular channel during adolescence
It is wide in youth and may become obliterated in old age
It widens progressively in every older adult
It is always completely obliterated at birth

correctAnswer.text: It is wide in youth and may become obliterated in old age

questions.explanation: The chapter describes the appendiceal lumen as wide in youth and usually obliterated in old age. This is a general anatomical observation rather than an absolute rule, so imaging interpretation should rely on direct findings and clinical context rather than age alone.

questions.question: What proportion of appendices may show calcification in the form of an appendicolith on plain radiography, according to the chapter?
questions.explanation: The chapter notes calcification in about 10% of cases, termed an appendicolith. An appendicolith can support the diagnosis in the appropriate setting, but its absence does not exclude appendicitis and its presence must be interpreted alongside appendiceal calibre, wall changes and surrounding inflammation.

questions.question: What is the approximate visibility of a normal appendix on ultrasound cited in the chapter?
questions.explanation: The chapter notes that a normal appendix is visible on ultrasound in about 60% of cases. Nonvisualization is therefore not equivalent to a normal examination; the result must be interpreted with secondary signs, patient habitus, bowel gas and the clinical probability of appendicitis.

questions.question: Which imaging feature is most useful for identifying the appendix on CT?

options.text: A vessel entering the porta hepatis
A structure that continues directly into the stomach
A loop that opens into the rectum
A blind-ending tubular structure arising from the caecum

correctAnswer.text: A blind-ending tubular structure arising from the caecum

questions.explanation: The appendix is identified by tracing a blind-ending tubular structure to its origin from the caecum. Because the tip can be retrocaecal, pelvic or otherwise displaced, tracing the structure to its base is more reliable than expecting it to occupy one fixed location.

questions.question: Which colonic landmark helps distinguish the caecum from the terminal ileum?

options.text: The ileocaecal valve at the junction of terminal ileum and caecum

correctAnswer.text: The ileocaecal valve at the junction of terminal ileum and caecum

questions.explanation: The ileocaecal valve marks the junction between terminal ileum and caecum. On CT and contrast studies, recognizing this junction helps orient the right lower quadrant and trace the appendix, caecum and terminal ileum as separate but adjacent structures.

questions.question: Which arterial branch supplies the proximal two-thirds of the transverse colon in the chapter?
questions.explanation: The chapter assigns the proximal two-thirds of the transverse colon to the middle colic artery, a branch of the superior mesenteric artery. The distal third belongs to the hindgut territory and receives supply via the left colic system, so the transverse colon spans two vascular territories.

questions.question: Which vessel supplies the distal transverse colon through the marginal arterial pathway described?

options.text: The ascending branch of the left colic artery

correctAnswer.text: The ascending branch of the left colic artery

questions.explanation: The distal transverse colon is supplied through the ascending branch of the left colic artery and the marginal artery. This corresponds to the hindgut territory and is a useful anatomical distinction when considering watershed regions and collateral circulation in the colon.

questions.question: What is the principal imaging difference between colonic haustra and small-bowel valvulae conniventes?

options.text: Haustra are always more closely spaced and cross the whole lumen
Valvulae conniventes are found only in the rectum
Haustra are sacculations that generally do not cross the full lumen, unlike small-bowel folds
The colon has no mucosal or wall pattern

correctAnswer.text: Haustra are sacculations that generally do not cross the full lumen, unlike small-bowel folds

questions.explanation: Colonic haustra form sacculations and generally do not cross the entire lumen, unlike the transverse valvulae conniventes of small bowel. This distinction helps identify bowel segments on plain films and contrast studies, although distension and projection can alter how clearly the pattern is seen.

questions.question: Which relationship of the hepatic flexure is described in the chapter?

options.text: It makes an impression on the inferior surface of the liver
It lies behind the sacrum in the pelvis
It passes through the diaphragmatic hiatus with the oesophagus
It is embedded within the spleen

correctAnswer.text: It makes an impression on the inferior surface of the liver

questions.explanation: The hepatic flexure lies near the inferior surface of the liver and can make an impression on it. It is also related to the right kidney, second part of the duodenum and gallbladder, making this region important when localizing disease in the right upper abdomen.

questions.question: Which structure lies posterior to the hepatic flexure in the relations described?

options.text: The lower pole of the right kidney

correctAnswer.text: The lower pole of the right kidney

questions.explanation: The chapter describes the lower pole of the right kidney posterior to the hepatic flexure. The duodenum and gallbladder are medial/anteromedial relations and the liver lies superiorly, so these neighboring structures help orient the flexure on axial and coronal CT.

questions.question: Which structures are described as medial or anteromedial to the hepatic flexure?

options.text: The second part of the duodenum and gallbladder
The descending thoracic aorta and left atrium

correctAnswer.text: The second part of the duodenum and gallbladder

questions.explanation: The hepatic flexure is related medially to the second part of the duodenum and anteromedially to the gallbladder. Because these organs lie close together, inflammatory or neoplastic disease may involve adjacent planes; cross-sectional imaging helps define the organ of origin.

questions.question: Which colonic segment is attached to the stomach by the gastrocolic ligament?
questions.explanation: The chapter notes that the transverse colon is attached to the stomach by the gastrocolic ligament. This peritoneal relationship explains the close proximity of the greater curvature and transverse colon and is relevant when describing the greater omentum and potential routes of disease spread.

questions.question: Which structure is typically located immediately before the sigmoid colon in the large-bowel sequence?
questions.explanation: The large bowel proceeds from caecum and ascending colon through the transverse and descending colon to the sigmoid colon, rectum and anal canal. This sequence is basic but important when tracing bowel on CT, especially when loops are redundant or displaced.

questions.question: Which structure is described as lying anterior to the sigmoid colon in males?
questions.explanation: The chapter describes the bladder anterior to the sigmoid colon in males; in females, the uterus also affects the anterior pelvic relationships. These relationships vary with bladder filling and pelvic organ position, so multiplanar imaging is useful for identifying the sigmoid colon in the pelvis.

questions.question: Which structures may lie anterior to the sigmoid colon in females according to the chapter?
questions.explanation: The chapter lists the bladder and uterus anterior to the sigmoid colon in females. The sigmoid is mobile and may occupy different pelvic positions, so the relationship is a guide rather than an invariant configuration in every scan.

questions.question: Which structure is described as posterior to the sigmoid colon?

options.text: The left psoas and lateral border of the aorta

correctAnswer.text: The left psoas and lateral border of the aorta

questions.explanation: The chapter describes the left psoas and lateral border of the aorta posterior to the sigmoid colon. In the pelvis, the sigmoid also relates to the pelvic side wall and adjacent reproductive structures, making its position variable on imaging.

questions.question: What is the mesorectum?

options.text: The mesentery of the appendix only
The fatty tissue surrounding the rectum, important in rectal cancer assessment
The peritoneal covering of the liver
The mucosal fold at the pylorus

correctAnswer.text: The fatty tissue surrounding the rectum, important in rectal cancer assessment

questions.explanation: The mesorectum is the fat-containing tissue surrounding the rectum. The chapter emphasizes its importance in rectal cancer assessment because tumour extension into this compartment and its relationship to the mesorectal fascia affect local staging and surgical planning.

questions.question: Why is MRI important in rectal cancer assessment as described in the chapter?

options.text: It can only show intraluminal gas
It is used exclusively to assess gastric emptying
It replaces all histology and endoscopy
It demonstrates the rectum and mesorectum for local tumour staging

correctAnswer.text: It demonstrates the rectum and mesorectum for local tumour staging

questions.explanation: MRI provides high soft-tissue contrast for evaluating the rectal wall, mesorectum and surrounding pelvic structures. The mesorectum is specifically highlighted as important in rectal cancer assessment, where defining the local extent of disease informs treatment planning.

questions.question: Which structure lies posterior to the rectum according to the chapter?

options.text: The presacral fascia and lower three sacral vertebrae

correctAnswer.text: The presacral fascia and lower three sacral vertebrae

questions.explanation: The rectum is posteriorly related to the presacral fascia and lower sacral vertebrae. This posterior plane is important on pelvic MRI, particularly when assessing tumour extension, presacral disease or the relationship of the rectum to the sacrum.

questions.question: Which structure may lie anterior to the rectum in females?

options.text: The vagina, with the rectovaginal septum between them

correctAnswer.text: The vagina, with the rectovaginal septum between them

questions.explanation: In females, the vagina lies anterior to the rectum, with a rectovaginal plane separating them. The bladder and uterus also contribute to anterior pelvic relationships at different levels; sagittal MRI is particularly useful for understanding these layered relationships.

questions.question: What does a rectocele describe in the chapter?

options.text: Anterior bulging of the rectal wall associated with pelvic floor weakness or descent
A congenital rotation of the midgut
A herniation of the appendix into the liver

correctAnswer.text: Anterior bulging of the rectal wall associated with pelvic floor weakness or descent

questions.explanation: The chapter describes a rectocele as anterior bulging of the rectal wall related to pelvic floor weakness or descent. Dynamic or dedicated pelvic imaging can help assess the compartment involved and associated pelvic floor abnormalities rather than treating it as a simple static bowel-wall lesion.

questions.question: Which imaging technique is highlighted for assessment of the anorectum and pelvic floor relationships?
questions.explanation: MRI is highlighted for anorectal assessment, including cancer staging and pelvic floor anatomy. Its multiplanar soft-tissue depiction helps show the rectal wall, mesorectum, sphincter complex and neighboring pelvic organs.

questions.question: Which two sphincters are described at the anal canal, with different types of control?

options.text: An involuntary internal sphincter and a voluntary external sphincter

correctAnswer.text: An involuntary internal sphincter and a voluntary external sphincter

questions.explanation: The internal anal sphincter is under involuntary control and the external anal sphincter is under voluntary control. Their different muscular composition and innervation matter when evaluating continence mechanisms and sphincter injury on endoanal ultrasound or MRI.

questions.question: Which nerve supply is described for the internal anal sphincter?
questions.explanation: The chapter associates the internal sphincter with the hypogastric plexus. This autonomic supply aligns with its involuntary control, whereas the external sphincter receives somatic innervation through branches related to the pudendal nerve.

questions.question: Which nerve is associated with the external anal sphincter in the chapter?

options.text: The inferior branch of the internal pudendal nerve

correctAnswer.text: The inferior branch of the internal pudendal nerve

questions.explanation: The chapter describes the external sphincter as supplied by the inferior branch of the internal pudendal nerve. This somatic innervation is consistent with voluntary control and is relevant when evaluating sphincter damage or planning interventions in the perineum.

questions.question: Which structure contributes to the pelvic diaphragm and supports the anorectal region?

options.text: The diaphragm of the thorax only

questions.explanation: The levator ani forms a major component of the pelvic diaphragm and supports pelvic viscera, including the anorectal region. The chapter describes components arising from the pubic bone, pelvic fascia over obturator internus and ischial spine region, which are useful landmarks in pelvic floor anatomy.

questions.question: Which muscle is identified as part of the levator ani arising from the pubic bone?
questions.explanation: The chapter names pubococcygeus as a component arising from the pubic bone. It also describes iliococcygeus and related pelvic floor structures; together these muscles support pelvic organs and influence the configuration of the pelvic floor around the rectum and anal canal.

questions.question: Which fascia lies posterior to the rectum and is relevant to the presacral plane?
questions.explanation: The presacral fascia is posterior to the rectum and overlies the sacral region. It is an important anatomical plane on MRI and surgery because the rectum is separated from the lower sacral vertebrae by this fascial tissue and intervening structures.

questions.question: Which portion of the anal canal is covered by mucosa according to the chapter?

options.text: Only the external sphincter is mucosal

questions.explanation: The chapter describes the upper two-thirds of the anal canal as mucosa-covered and the lower portion as skin-covered. This transition reflects different epithelial and sensory territories and is relevant when interpreting the anatomy of the anal canal and perianal region.

questions.question: What is a continuing role of barium studies in GI imaging according to the chapter?

options.text: They remain diagnostic tools and problem-solving examinations alongside CT or MRI
They have no role in modern imaging
They are used only to image the brain

correctAnswer.text: They remain diagnostic tools and problem-solving examinations alongside CT or MRI

questions.explanation: The chapter states that barium studies remain widely used as diagnostic tools or in conjunction with CT and MRI as problem-solving examinations. They are particularly useful for luminal contour, transit and mucosal patterns, while cross-sectional imaging provides surrounding anatomy and extraluminal assessment.

questions.question: What does a barium follow-through primarily demonstrate?

options.text: The renal cortex without bowel opacification
Only the arterial supply of the liver
The passage and appearance of contrast through the small bowel
The sphincter muscles of the eye

correctAnswer.text: The passage and appearance of contrast through the small bowel

questions.explanation: A barium follow-through traces contrast through the small bowel and depicts loops, fold pattern and the ileocaecal region. It is a luminal examination and should be understood alongside CT or MRI when mural, mesenteric or extraintestinal disease is a concern.

questions.question: Which landmark can be used to orient the distal small bowel on contrast studies?
questions.explanation: The ileocaecal valve and caecum mark the transition from terminal ileum to large bowel. Identifying this region helps establish which loops are distal ileum and which are caecum or colon, especially when the loops overlap on projectional imaging.

questions.question: What is the expected appearance of a normally distended bowel wall compared with a collapsed loop on enterography?

options.text: Distension always makes the wall appear massively thickened
Distension thins the wall and separates loops, improving assessment
Collapsed loops are always easier to assess

correctAnswer.text: Distension thins the wall and separates loops, improving assessment

questions.explanation: Adequate distension stretches the bowel wall and separates adjacent loops, making abnormal thickening and narrowing easier to recognize. Collapsed loops may appear falsely thick and can be difficult to distinguish from pathology, which is why enterography technique is central to interpretation.

questions.question: Which of the following best explains why ultrasound is useful for paediatric intussusception?

options.text: It can focus on bowel morphology and demonstrate the affected segment without ionizing radiation
It requires no operator skill or clinical context
It is the only modality that shows any abdominal anatomy

correctAnswer.text: It can focus on bowel morphology and demonstrate the affected segment without ionizing radiation

questions.explanation: Ultrasound is a focused tool for paediatric intussusception and avoids ionizing radiation. Its value lies in real-time visualization of bowel morphology; the examination remains dependent on technique and must be interpreted with the clinical picture.

questions.question: Which anatomical relationship explains why pancreatic-head disease can affect the second part of the duodenum?

options.text: The second part lies in the left pleural cavity
The second part passes through the spleen
The second duodenal part lies closely alongside the pancreatic head
The duodenum is separated from the pancreas by the pelvis

correctAnswer.text: The second duodenal part lies closely alongside the pancreatic head

questions.explanation: The second part of the duodenum descends alongside the pancreatic head, with the biliary and pancreatic ducts entering its medial wall. This close relationship explains why pathology in one structure can alter or compress the other and why CT/MRI should evaluate both together.

questions.question: Which vessel is a key landmark at the third part of the duodenum?

options.text: The superior mesenteric artery and vein

correctAnswer.text: The superior mesenteric artery and vein

questions.explanation: The third duodenal part crosses anterior to the aorta and is related to the superior mesenteric vessels. Their position can create an indentation and is an important landmark when evaluating the duodenum and surrounding retroperitoneal anatomy.

questions.question: Which statement best describes the relationship between embryology and adult bowel position?

options.text: The rotation places the caecum in the thorax normally
Rotation leaves the entire bowel in the midline without positional organization
Normal midgut rotation places jejunum and the duodenojejunal flexure left of midline and proximal colon to the right
Adult bowel position is unrelated to embryological rotation

correctAnswer.text: Normal midgut rotation places jejunum and the duodenojejunal flexure left of midline and proximal colon to the right

questions.explanation: The chapter links the 270-degree anticlockwise rotation of the midgut with the adult arrangement of jejunum and the duodenojejunal flexure to the left and proximal colon to the right. This developmental explanation helps interpret malrotation when bowel positions are reversed or the mesenteric root is abnormally short.

questions.question: Why should a nonvisualized appendix on ultrasound not be treated as definitive exclusion of appendicitis?

options.text: The appendix is always behind the liver
Ultrasound cannot image any part of the right lower quadrant
A normal appendix is visible in only about 60% of cases in the chapter

correctAnswer.text: A normal appendix is visible in only about 60% of cases in the chapter

questions.explanation: The chapter reports that the normal appendix is visualized on ultrasound in about 60% of cases. Because nonvisualization is common, the examiner should consider secondary inflammatory signs and clinical probability rather than equating an unseen appendix with a negative study.

questions.question: Which feature of the transverse colon is important when describing its peritoneal relationship?

options.text: It is attached to the stomach by the gastrocolic ligament and has a mesocolon
It is continuous with the oesophagus
It is fixed directly to the sacrum without mobility
It lies within the renal collecting system

correctAnswer.text: It is attached to the stomach by the gastrocolic ligament and has a mesocolon

questions.explanation: The transverse colon has a mesocolon and is attached to the stomach by the gastrocolic ligament. These peritoneal attachments allow mobility and create an anatomical route between the greater curvature and transverse colon, which is relevant to the spread of fluid or disease.

questions.question: Which structure is most useful to identify first when tracing the appendix on cross-sectional imaging?
questions.explanation: Because the appendix is variable in position, identifying the caecum and tracing the appendix from its posteromedial wall is more dependable than searching for the tip in a presumed location. This approach reduces the chance of confusing an adjacent small-bowel loop with the appendix.

questions.question: Which organ is directly related to the hepatic flexure superiorly?

options.text: The right lobe of the liver

correctAnswer.text: The right lobe of the liver

questions.explanation: The right lobe of the liver lies superior to the hepatic flexure, and the flexure may impress the liver’s inferior surface. This relationship is a useful landmark in the right upper abdomen and helps distinguish the hepatic from the splenic flexure.

questions.question: Which structure is adjacent to the left colic flexure superiorly?
questions.explanation: The splenic or left colic flexure lies close to the spleen and is a transition between transverse and descending colon. It is relatively high in the left upper abdomen, and its proximity to the spleen and left kidney is useful when orienting coronal and axial images.

questions.question: Which organ is described as posterior to the splenic flexure?
questions.explanation: The left kidney lies posterior to the splenic flexure according to the chapter. The spleen is superior to the flexure, and the descending colon continues inferiorly; these relationships help localize the flexure when the colon is gas-filled or displaced.

questions.question: What is the purpose of evaluating the mesorectal fascia in rectal MRI?

options.text: To assess the local extent of rectal disease in relation to the surgical plane
To measure the diameter of the common bile duct

correctAnswer.text: To assess the local extent of rectal disease in relation to the surgical plane

questions.explanation: The mesorectal compartment and its fascia are important in local rectal cancer staging because tumour spread toward the fascia affects surgical planning. MRI depicts these soft-tissue planes more clearly than projectional studies and helps characterize the relationship of tumour to surrounding tissue.

questions.question: Which statement best distinguishes a luminal contrast study from CT or MRI?

options.text: Contrast studies emphasize lumen contour and transit, while CT/MRI show bowel and surrounding anatomy
Contrast studies show all extraintestinal tissues better than MRI
CT cannot show the bowel wall

correctAnswer.text: Contrast studies emphasize lumen contour and transit, while CT/MRI show bowel and surrounding anatomy

questions.explanation: Barium studies provide detailed luminal contour and transit information, whereas CT and MRI demonstrate the bowel wall, mesentery and neighboring organs. The chapter presents these methods as complementary rather than interchangeable, with the choice determined by the clinical question.

questions.question: Which set of structures makes the gastro-oesophageal junction a recognizable landmark on cross-sectional imaging?

options.text: Distal oesophagus, gastric cardia/fundus and adjacent diaphragm
Rectum, anal canal and pubic symphysis
Pancreatic tail, spleen and left kidney only

correctAnswer.text: Distal oesophagus, gastric cardia/fundus and adjacent diaphragm

questions.explanation: The gastro-oesophageal junction is where the distal oesophagus enters the stomach near the diaphragm. Recognizing the distal oesophagus and adjacent gastric cardia/fundus on sagittal and axial images helps orient the upper GI tract and distinguish it from adjacent mediastinal structures.

questions.question: Which statement about the oesophageal outer wall is supported by the chapter’s layer description?

options.text: The oesophagus has an outer adventitia rather than a continuous serosal coat
It is lined by peritoneum along its entire length
It is surrounded by articular cartilage

correctAnswer.text: The oesophagus has an outer adventitia rather than a continuous serosal coat

questions.explanation: The chapter labels the outer oesophageal layer as adventitia. This differs from the serosal covering of many intraperitoneal GI segments and is relevant to the anatomical routes by which oesophageal disease can extend into surrounding tissues.

questions.question: Which structures are included in the chapter’s description of the small bowel’s course?

options.text: From the duodenojejunal flexure to the ileocaecal junction
From the pylorus directly to the anal verge
From the pharynx to the gastro-oesophageal junction
From the caecum to the rectum only

correctAnswer.text: From the duodenojejunal flexure to the ileocaecal junction

questions.explanation: The small bowel continues from the duodenojejunal flexure through jejunum and ileum to the ileocaecal junction. These transition points are more useful on imaging than attempting to identify an isolated loop by location alone, because small-bowel loops are mobile and overlap.

questions.question: What is the significance of the appendix being very mobile?

options.text: It has no relationship to the caecum
It is always visible on plain radiographs
Its tip can occupy variable positions, which changes imaging appearance and sometimes symptom location

correctAnswer.text: Its tip can occupy variable positions, which changes imaging appearance and sometimes symptom location

questions.explanation: The chapter emphasizes that the appendix is very mobile, commonly retrocaecal but potentially located elsewhere. This variability affects ultrasound visibility and the distribution of local inflammatory change, so imaging should trace the appendix rather than assume a fixed pelvic or anterior position.

questions.question: Which bowel segment is directly associated with the ileocaecal valve?
questions.explanation: The ileocaecal valve is the junction where terminal ileum enters the caecum. It is a key orientation landmark for the right lower quadrant and helps distinguish terminal ileal loops from caecum and proximal colon on CT and contrast examinations.

questions.question: Which embryological structure gives rise to the ureter, renal pelvis, calyces and collecting tubules?
questions.explanation: The chapter describes the ureteric bud arising from the mesonephric duct and developing into the ureter and collecting system, including the renal pelvis, calyces and collecting tubules. The metanephric mesenchyme contributes the renal parenchymal components that interact with the bud. Keeping these origins distinct helps explain why abnormal bud development produces collecting-system and ureteric variants.

questions.question: Failure of formation of which structure is identified as a cause of renal agenesis in the chapter?
questions.explanation: The chapter’s diagram links an absent kidney to an absent ureteric bud. The bud is required to induce and organize development of the metanephric kidney; without it, a kidney does not form. This differs from an ectopic kidney, in which renal tissue develops but fails to ascend normally.

questions.question: What developmental event most directly explains a pelvic kidney?

options.text: Persistence of the fetal adrenal cortex
Failure of normal ascent from the pelvis

correctAnswer.text: Failure of normal ascent from the pelvis

questions.explanation: The chapter describes a pelvic kidney as resulting from migratory arrest. The kidney remains low rather than reaching its usual upper retroperitoneal position, and its vascular supply may arise from pelvic vessels, including the internal iliac artery. This is a positional anomaly, not renal agenesis.

questions.question: What is the defining fusion pattern of a horseshoe kidney described in the chapter?

options.text: Fusion of the upper poles within the thorax
Fusion of the lower poles across the midline
Fusion of the renal pelves without parenchymal connection

correctAnswer.text: Fusion of the lower poles across the midline

questions.explanation: A horseshoe kidney classically results when the lower poles fuse across the midline. During ascent, the fused kidney is commonly arrested by the inferior mesenteric artery, so the renal tissue lies lower than expected. On imaging, the isthmus may cross anterior to the great vessels.

questions.question: Which syndrome associations are specifically mentioned for horseshoe kidney?
questions.explanation: The chapter notes that horseshoe kidney is the commonest renal fusion anomaly and is associated with Turner syndrome and trisomy 18. These associations are useful when a fused renal configuration is found, although the imaging appearance alone does not establish a chromosomal diagnosis.

questions.question: What is meant by crossed renal ectopia?

options.text: The renal pelvis enters the bladder directly
A kidney rotates without changing sides
A kidney crosses to the opposite side, often with fusion to the normally positioned kidney

correctAnswer.text: A kidney crosses to the opposite side, often with fusion to the normally positioned kidney

questions.explanation: In crossed renal ectopia, one kidney crosses the midline; the chapter illustrates crossed fused ectopia in which the ectopic kidney fuses with the normally positioned kidney. Despite the abnormal renal position, the ureteric orifices remain in their usual bladder locations, an important clue on urography.

questions.question: In a complete duplex collecting system, what developmental arrangement is described?

options.text: The ureter fuses with the renal artery
One ureteric bud fails to branch
Two ureteric buds produce two separate ureters and two bladder orifices
The renal pelvis develops without calyces

correctAnswer.text: Two ureteric buds produce two separate ureters and two bladder orifices

questions.explanation: The chapter distinguishes complete duplication, caused by two ureteric buds and resulting in separate ureters and bladder orifices, from partial duplication, where a single ureter bifurcates early. This distinction matters because the insertion and drainage pattern of each moiety can differ.

questions.question: A single ureter divides into two branches high in its course. How is this classified?
questions.explanation: A partial duplex system occurs when one ureteric bud/ureter divides early, leaving a common distal ureter. In a complete duplex system, two separate ureters extend to separate bladder orifices. Imaging should therefore assess whether the duplication persists all the way to the bladder.

questions.question: According to the Weigert–Meyer rule, where does the upper-pole ureter in a duplex system tend to insert?

options.text: More cranially than the lower-pole ureter in every case
Into the ureteropelvic junction of the lower moiety

questions.explanation: The chapter states that the upper-pole ureter tends to have a more caudal, ectopic insertion and may occasionally enter the urethra or vagina. The upper-pole moiety is consequently prone to obstruction or ureterocele. By contrast, the lower-pole ureter tends to reflux because its intramural course is less oblique and less competent.

questions.question: Which duplex-system moiety is described as more prone to vesicoureteric reflux?

options.text: Both moieties are always equally affected

questions.explanation: The chapter explains that the lower-pole ureter tends to reflux because it has a less oblique and potentially incompetent passage through the bladder wall. The upper-pole ureter more often has ectopic insertion, obstruction or a ureterocele. This is a useful pattern, not an absolute rule for every patient.

questions.question: What is a ureterocele?

options.text: Fusion of the renal lower poles
Dilatation of the intramural distal ureter
A cyst arising from the adrenal cortex

correctAnswer.text: Dilatation of the intramural distal ureter

questions.explanation: The chapter defines a ureterocele as dilatation of the intramural ureter. It is particularly relevant in duplex systems, where the upper-pole ureter may be obstructed. Urographic or cross-sectional imaging may show a rounded filling defect at the bladder end of the ureter.

questions.question: Which renal anomaly is associated with a kidney crossing to the opposite side and fusion with the other kidney, while ureteric orifices remain normally located?
questions.explanation: Crossed fused ectopia combines abnormal migration across the midline with fusion to the contralateral kidney. The chapter emphasizes that the ureteric orifices remain normally sited, so tracing the ureters can clarify an otherwise confusing renal arrangement. Aberrant vascular supply is also expected.

questions.question: What is the developmental basis of a supernumerary kidney in the chapter’s diagram?

options.text: The renal capsule duplicates after birth
The adrenal gland divides into two limbs

questions.explanation: The diagram links two ureteric buds with a supernumerary kidney and ureter. This differs from a duplex collecting system, where a single kidney has duplicated drainage anatomy. Distinguishing additional renal tissue from duplicated collecting structures is important for describing the anomaly accurately.

questions.question: What explains an over-rotated kidney with the renal pelvis facing anterolaterally?

options.text: A stone lodged at the pelviureteric junction

questions.explanation: During ascent, the kidney normally rotates so that the hilum and pelvis face medially. The chapter illustrates an over-rotated kidney whose pelvis faces anterolaterally. Recognizing this orientation prevents the collecting system from being mistaken for a mass or incorrectly described as the normal configuration.

questions.question: Why can a pelvic or ectopic kidney have an unusual arterial supply?

options.text: The adrenal artery replaces all renal arteries
Renal arteries arise only after the kidney reaches its final position
It may retain vessels acquired at a lower level during ascent
The kidney receives its entire supply from the portal vein

correctAnswer.text: It may retain vessels acquired at a lower level during ascent

questions.explanation: As the kidney ascends, it recruits successively higher arterial branches while lower vessels normally involute. If ascent is arrested, vessels from a lower level may persist; the chapter specifically notes internal iliac supply for pelvic kidneys. This embryology explains the frequency of variant vessels in ectopic kidneys.

questions.question: What can a plain abdominal radiograph directly show about the kidney, according to the chapter?

options.text: The renal cortex and medulla separately
The renal outline when it is outlined by surrounding fat
The non-opacified ureters throughout their course
The individual calyces in every patient

correctAnswer.text: The renal outline when it is outlined by surrounding fat

questions.explanation: On plain films, intrarenal anatomy is not visible. The renal edge may be seen because surrounding perirenal fat provides contrast, but the ureters are not visible when they are not opacified. A visible renal outline should therefore not be mistaken for assessment of internal renal structure.

questions.question: What approximate kidney length is given for plain radiographic assessment?

options.text: About 11–15 cm, or roughly 3.5 vertebral body heights

correctAnswer.text: About 11–15 cm, or roughly 3.5 vertebral body heights

questions.explanation: The chapter gives a typical kidney length of about 11–15 cm, approximately 3.5 vertebral bodies. It also cautions that renal size is magnified by around 15% on radiographs and that a ptotic kidney may appear foreshortened because it lies posteriorly. Projection and position therefore affect apparent size.

questions.question: Why might a ptotic kidney appear foreshortened on a radiograph?

options.text: It becomes intrinsically shorter in every case
Its collecting system is always obstructed
It lies more posteriorly and is projected obliquely

correctAnswer.text: It lies more posteriorly and is projected obliquely

questions.explanation: The chapter notes that ptotic kidneys may appear foreshortened because they flop posteriorly. This is a projectional effect rather than proof of reduced renal length. Cross-sectional imaging can clarify the true dimensions and position when plain-film measurements are uncertain.

questions.question: Which modality is described as useful for evaluating renal size, parenchyma, collecting-system dilatation, masses and calculi without ionizing radiation?
questions.explanation: Ultrasound provides multiplanar assessment of renal size and parenchyma and can readily identify collecting-system dilatation, masses and calculi. Its limitations include acoustic access and less complete anatomical detail than CT in some settings. The chapter also notes that the normal adrenal is much easier to see in neonates than in adults.

questions.question: During which IVU phase is renal parenchymal outline best assessed after intravenous contrast?

options.text: The phase before contrast reaches the kidneys

questions.explanation: The chapter describes the early or nephrographic phase as the phase in which renal parenchyma and its outline can be assessed. The later urographic phase opacifies the collecting system and ureters. Recognizing the phase helps match the observed anatomy to the structure being evaluated.

questions.question: Which IVU phase is most useful for delineating the collecting system and ureters?
questions.explanation: In the urographic phase, excreted contrast outlines the pelvicalyceal systems and ureters. The nephrographic phase instead emphasizes renal parenchyma. This distinction is central to interpreting IVU images and also informs the timing of CT urography acquisitions.

questions.question: Which investigation is specifically noted as replacing IVU in many contemporary applications?

options.text: Adrenal scintigraphy for all renal conditions
Ultrasound in every adult regardless of indication
CT and MRI, with CT urography used for urinary tract assessment

correctAnswer.text: CT and MRI, with CT urography used for urinary tract assessment

questions.explanation: The chapter states that CT and MRI are replacing IVU. Unenhanced CT is particularly useful for urinary calculi, while CT urography depicts the urinary tract and cross-sectional anatomy. Modality selection still depends on the clinical question, radiation considerations and patient factors.

questions.question: For detection and assessment of urinary calculi, which modality does the chapter identify as stronger?
questions.explanation: The chapter explicitly contrasts CT’s strength for renal calculi with MRI’s strength for characterization of renal cysts. Unenhanced CT KUB is especially useful because stones are conspicuous without contrast obscuring their attenuation. This is a modality-specific advantage, not a claim that MRI has no urinary applications.

questions.question: Which modality is described as particularly useful for characterization of renal cysts?

options.text: Colour Doppler of the adrenal gland only

questions.explanation: The chapter identifies MRI as better for renal cyst characterization, while CT provides precise anatomy and is strong for calculi. MRI tissue contrast can help characterize cyst contents and distinguish simple from more complex lesions when appropriate sequences are obtained.

questions.question: What is a key advantage of CT anatomy over MRI emphasized in the chapter?

options.text: More precise anatomical detail from near-isotropic spatial data
Superior visualization of every stone regardless of protocol
Direct measurement of renal function without contrast

correctAnswer.text: More precise anatomical detail from near-isotropic spatial data

questions.explanation: The chapter notes that anatomical information is more precise on CT because of virtual isotropic data. Thin-section multiplanar reconstructions can show vessels, collecting systems and surrounding structures in detail. MRI remains complementary, particularly for selected tissue-characterization questions and when radiation avoidance matters.

questions.question: On ultrasound, how is the normal kidney described relative to the liver?

options.text: The renal cortex and medulla cannot be distinguished at all
The kidney is always markedly hyperechoic to the liver
The kidney has no visible parenchyma
The kidney is hypoechoic compared with the liver

correctAnswer.text: The kidney is hypoechoic compared with the liver

questions.explanation: The chapter’s imaging summary describes the kidney as hypoechoic compared with the liver on ultrasound. Normal renal ultrasound also allows assessment of corticomedullary differentiation and collecting-system dilatation. Echogenicity should be interpreted with the patient and technical setting in mind, not as an isolated diagnosis.
