questions.question: What does a longitudinal renal ultrasound normally allow the examiner to assess?

options.text: All segmental renal arteries with CT-level detail
The full course of every non-dilated ureter in all patients
The adrenal gland reliably in every adult

questions.explanation: The chapter illustrates normal corticomedullary differentiation on longitudinal ultrasound. Ultrasound is a useful first-line examination for size and parenchymal appearance, but it does not consistently show the entire non-dilated ureter and is less detailed than CT for complex vascular anatomy.

questions.question: Between which vertebral levels does the chapter place the kidneys in the retroperitoneum?
questions.explanation: The chapter places the kidneys in the retroperitoneum between T12 and L4. Their exact levels vary with respiration, body habitus and position. The right kidney is usually lower because of the liver, so side-to-side asymmetry is a normal anatomical expectation rather than automatically a sign of disease.

questions.question: Why is the right kidney usually lower than the left?

options.text: The right renal artery is longer
The spleen pushes the left kidney down
The right adrenal gland pulls the kidney down

questions.explanation: The chapter states that the right kidney is more inferior because it is displaced by the liver, in approximately three quarters of cases. The left kidney may be up to 1.5 cm longer. Normal variation exists, so the relationship should be interpreted with overall renal position and morphology.

questions.question: Which kidney may be up to 1.5 cm longer according to the chapter?

options.text: Neither kidney has a predictable size range
The right kidney in every individual
Both kidneys are always identical in length

questions.explanation: The chapter gives average renal dimensions and notes that the left kidney may be up to 1.5 cm longer than the right. This complements the common finding that the right kidney sits lower because of the liver. Small asymmetry alone is therefore not necessarily pathological.

questions.question: What is the usual average renal length stated in the chapter’s gross anatomy section?
questions.explanation: The gross anatomy section gives an average kidney length of 9–12 cm, with breadth around 5–7.5 cm and thickness around 2.5 cm. These are approximate adult dimensions, not rigid diagnostic cutoffs. Imaging measurements vary with technique, body size and the plane in which the kidney is measured.

questions.question: Which kidney orientation is described in the sagittal plane?

options.text: The upper pole always faces directly anteriorly
The upper pole faces more posteriorly
The lower pole faces into the vertebral canal
The renal hilum faces laterally in all individuals

correctAnswer.text: The upper pole faces more posteriorly

questions.explanation: The chapter notes that each kidney lies obliquely and that, in the sagittal plane, the upper pole faces more posteriorly. This obliquity is important when interpreting axial imaging because the renal long axis does not align perfectly with the body’s cranio-caudal axis.

questions.question: Which structures are listed among the contents of the renal hilum/sinus region?

options.text: Renal vein, renal artery, ureter, lymphatics, sympathetic fibres and fat
Portal vein, hepatic duct and bile duct
Splenic vein, pancreatic duct and stomach
Femoral artery, femoral vein and femoral nerve

correctAnswer.text: Renal vein, renal artery, ureter, lymphatics, sympathetic fibres and fat

questions.explanation: The chapter lists the renal vein, renal artery, ureter, lymphatic and sympathetic fibres, and fat among the hilar contents. The arrangement of vessels and collecting system must be assessed in cross-section rather than assuming a single fixed relationship across all patients and variants.

questions.question: What is the tough fibro-elastic covering directly surrounding the kidney called?
questions.explanation: The kidney is directly bound by a tough fibro-elastic capsule. This should be distinguished from the renal fascia, which encloses the perinephric space and adjacent contents. The capsule closely invests the organ; the fascial planes are more external and are important for understanding the spread of fluid or disease.

questions.question: What is the functional unit of the kidney?
questions.explanation: The chapter identifies the nephron as the functional unit of the kidney. Nephrons filter blood and modify the filtrate before it enters the collecting system. The papilla, calyx and renal sinus are gross anatomical structures involved in drainage or containing hilar elements rather than the basic functional unit.

questions.question: How many collecting ducts are described as emptying into each papilla?
questions.explanation: The chapter states that about 10–20 collecting ducts empty into each papilla and calyx. The papilla projects into a minor calyx, allowing urine to drain from the collecting ducts into the calyceal system. This microscopic-to-gross relationship explains the organization seen on urographic imaging.

questions.question: What is the usual drainage sequence from the calyces toward the ureter?

options.text: Calyces drain through infundibula, which join to form the renal pelvis
Papillae drain directly into the bladder
The renal vein drains into the calyces before the pelvis
The ureter drains into the renal cortex

correctAnswer.text: Calyces drain through infundibula, which join to form the renal pelvis

questions.explanation: The chapter describes calyces draining into infundibula, which unite to form the renal pelvis. The pelvis then continues as the ureter. Recognizing this sequence helps localize a transition point when there is obstruction and prevents confusing a calyceal variant with a focal lesion.

questions.question: What is the distinction between a minor/simple calyx and a major/compound calyx in the chapter’s terminology?

options.text: A minor calyx is always outside the kidney
Minor calyces are renal arteries and major calyces are renal veins
They are synonyms for the renal cortex and medulla
Minor or simple calyces are the smaller calyces; larger compound calyces collect their drainage

correctAnswer.text: Minor or simple calyces are the smaller calyces; larger compound calyces collect their drainage

questions.explanation: The chapter describes minor or simple calyces as small calyces and contrasts them with major or compound calyces. Their number and configuration vary. On imaging, normal variation in calyceal arrangement should be distinguished from true dilatation or an obstructing filling defect.

questions.question: Which normal renal feature may persist from fetal life into adulthood?

options.text: A duplicated adrenal cortex in every adult
A renal pelvis that opens into the portal vein

questions.explanation: Fetal lobules usually regress during the first year after birth, but the chapter notes that they may persist into adult life. Persistent lobulation creates a gently lobulated renal contour and should not automatically be called scarring; scars more often have focal cortical thinning and associated parenchymal distortion.

questions.question: Which external contour finding can mimic renal scarring but is a normal variant?
questions.explanation: Persistent fetal lobulation can produce grooves between lobes on the renal surface. The chapter specifically cautions that this reflects fusion of fetal lobules and should not be confused with a scar. A scar is more likely to be focal and associated with cortical thinning, whereas fetal lobulation generally preserves the underlying contour smoothly.

questions.question: Into how many main spaces does the chapter divide the retroperitoneum?

options.text: Three: perinephric, anterior pararenal and posterior pararenal spaces
Four: cortical, medullary, calyceal and ureteric spaces
Five: hepatic, splenic, gastric, pelvic and renal spaces

correctAnswer.text: Three: perinephric, anterior pararenal and posterior pararenal spaces

questions.explanation: The chapter divides the retroperitoneum into the perinephric space and the anterior and posterior pararenal spaces. These spaces are defined by fascial boundaries and contain different structures. Understanding them helps explain the pathways by which blood, urine, inflammation or tumour can spread.

questions.question: Which fascia forms the anterior boundary of the perinephric space in the chapter’s description?

options.text: The parietal peritoneum directly covering the renal capsule

questions.explanation: Gerota’s fascia is identified as the anterior renal fascia, while Zuckerkandl’s fascia is the posterior renal fascia. Together they enclose the perinephric space around the kidney and adrenal region, although the chapter notes that the fascial boundaries and their medial attachments can be incomplete or variable.

questions.question: Which fascia forms the posterior boundary of the perinephric space?
questions.explanation: The posterior renal fascia is called Zuckerkandl’s fascia in the chapter. It passes behind the kidney and merges medially with fascia attached to the vertebral column. Its relationship to the anterior renal fascia helps define the perinephric compartment on CT.

questions.question: Which structure is located posterior to the kidney among the listed relations?

options.text: The stomach in direct contact throughout

questions.explanation: The chapter’s posterior relations include the diaphragm and ribs superiorly and the posterior abdominal wall musculature, including quadratus lumborum and psoas-related structures. These relationships are visible on axial CT and help orient the kidney relative to the spine and surrounding compartments.

questions.question: Which structure is an anterior relation of the right kidney specifically shown in the chapter?

options.text: The sigmoid mesentery as its sole anterior relation

questions.explanation: The chapter’s renal relations illustration labels the duodenum anterior to the right kidney. Other anterior relationships differ by side: the liver is important on the right, while the spleen, pancreas and splenic flexure are important on the left. Side-specific relations help localize disease and plan procedures.

questions.question: Which group best matches anterior relations of the left kidney listed in the chapter?

options.text: Caecum, appendix and ascending colon only
Adrenal gland, pancreas, splenic vessels, spleen and splenic flexure

correctAnswer.text: Adrenal gland, pancreas, splenic vessels, spleen and splenic flexure

questions.explanation: The chapter lists the adrenal gland, pancreas, splenic vessels, spleen and splenic flexure among the left kidney’s anterior relations. These structures explain why left renal pathology may contact or displace adjacent upper abdominal organs. The exact relationship varies with body habitus and organ position.

questions.question: Which space lies posterior to the perinephric space?
questions.explanation: The posterior pararenal space lies behind the perinephric compartment and is related to the posterior abdominal wall. The anterior pararenal space lies anterior to the perinephric compartment. These distinctions are useful when describing the location of retroperitoneal fluid or masses on CT.

questions.question: What proportion of cardiac output may be received by the renal arteries according to the chapter?
questions.explanation: The chapter notes that the kidneys receive up to 30% of cardiac output. This high flow supports filtration and makes renal perfusion highly relevant in contrast-enhanced imaging. The proportion is approximate and depends on physiological conditions; it should not be interpreted as a fixed value for every patient.

questions.question: Where does the main renal artery most commonly arise?
questions.explanation: The main renal arteries most commonly arise directly from the abdominal aorta and enter the renal hilum. The chapter emphasizes that accessory arteries are common, so vascular mapping is important before renal surgery, transplantation or endovascular intervention.

questions.question: How common are accessory renal arteries according to the chapter?
questions.explanation: Accessory renal arteries occur in about 20–25% of individuals in the chapter’s account. They are persistent vessels from the kidney’s ascent and may enter at the upper or lower pole rather than through the hilum. A lower-pole artery can be clinically important because it may supply a substantial segment and cross near the ureteropelvic junction.

questions.question: Why are accessory renal arteries embryologically understandable?

options.text: The kidney develops inside the heart
The renal artery normally migrates down from the neck
Lower-level arteries may persist while the kidney recruits higher arteries during ascent
Accessory arteries arise from the renal vein after birth

correctAnswer.text: Lower-level arteries may persist while the kidney recruits higher arteries during ascent

questions.explanation: During ascent, the kidney successively recruits more superior arterial branches while lower branches usually involute. Persistence of one or more lower vessels produces accessory arteries. This explains why the vessels are a common normal variant and why their origins and entry points should be documented on angiographic studies.

questions.question: Where does the main renal artery divide into segmental arteries, according to the chapter?

options.text: At the level of the common femoral artery
Only after reaching the adrenal gland

questions.explanation: The chapter describes the main renal artery dividing into segmental arteries near the hilum. Segmental branches then supply distinct renal territories. Because the segmental arteries behave as end arteries, occlusion can cause a defined region of infarction, and the branching pattern matters during surgery or embolization.

questions.question: Which branch is classically described as the first division of the main renal artery?
questions.explanation: The chapter states that the first division is classically a posterior segmental branch, after which the main artery divides into four further segmental branches. This is a typical pattern rather than an invariant arrangement; CT angiography can show patient-specific branching before intervention.

questions.question: Which statement best describes renal segmental arteries?

options.text: They are branches of the renal vein
They freely communicate through a large collateral network throughout the cortex
They drain lymph directly to the bladder
They are end arteries supplying defined territories

correctAnswer.text: They are end arteries supplying defined territories

questions.explanation: The chapter’s angiographic figure describes the smaller cortical arterial vessels as end arteries. Limited collateral communication means interruption of a segmental branch may produce segmental ischemia or infarction. This is why the exact arterial anatomy is important in partial nephrectomy and selective embolization.

questions.question: What is the general branching sequence of renal arterial vessels given in the chapter?

options.text: Portal, hepatic, splenic, cortical and calyceal branches
Arcuate, renal vein, ureter, segmental and aorta
Segmental, lobar, interlobar, arcuate and smaller cortical branches
Interlobar, bladder, gonadal, adrenal and urethral branches

correctAnswer.text: Segmental, lobar, interlobar, arcuate and smaller cortical branches

questions.explanation: The chapter describes segmental arteries branching into lobar arteries, which divide into interlobar branches; arcuate arteries then run along the bases of the pyramids and give rise to smaller cortical branches. Knowing this sequence relates the vascular tree to the renal pyramids and helps interpret Doppler and angiographic images.

questions.question: Where do interlobar arteries run in the kidney?
questions.explanation: Interlobar arteries pass between the renal pyramids, while arcuate arteries run along the bases of the pyramids. This spatial arrangement is shown in the chapter’s renal vascular illustrations and helps distinguish the vascular branches on Doppler ultrasound or contrast imaging.

questions.question: Which vessel is described as about three times longer than the right renal vein?
questions.explanation: The chapter states that the left renal vein is approximately three times longer than the right, with a length around 6–10 cm. It crosses toward the inferior vena cava and receives tributaries including the left adrenal and left gonadal veins. Its long course explains its exposure to compression and anatomical variants.

questions.question: Which tributaries of the left renal vein are specifically listed in the chapter?

options.text: Superior mesenteric and inferior mesenteric veins
Right adrenal vein and right gonadal vein in every case
Left adrenal vein and left gonadal vein

correctAnswer.text: Left adrenal vein and left gonadal vein

questions.explanation: The chapter lists the left adrenal vein and left gonadal vein among the tributaries of the left renal vein, with lumbar veins variably joining it. This differs from the right adrenal vein, which usually drains directly to the inferior vena cava, and the right gonadal vein, which also typically drains directly to the IVC.

questions.question: Which renal venous anomaly is identified as the commonest left renal vein anomaly in the chapter?

options.text: A right-sided renal vein with no IVC connection
A left renal vein draining into the splenic artery

questions.explanation: The chapter’s text gives the circumaortic left renal vein as a common left renal vein anomaly and describes anterior and posterior limbs encircling the aorta. The chapter’s figure captions report differing incidence figures across descriptions, so the key diagnostic feature is the two-limb course rather than relying on a single percentage.

questions.question: What defines a circumaortic left renal vein?

options.text: The right renal vein passes behind the liver
The left renal vein has anterior and posterior limbs that encircle the aorta
Both renal arteries pass through the bladder wall
The left renal vein terminates in the portal vein

correctAnswer.text: The left renal vein has anterior and posterior limbs that encircle the aorta

questions.explanation: A circumaortic left renal vein has anterior and posterior venous limbs around the aorta. The chapter illustrates both limbs draining to the IVC. Recognizing this variant is important before retroperitoneal surgery or venous intervention because an unrecognized posterior limb can be injured.

questions.question: What is the defining course of a retro-aortic left renal vein?

options.text: It passes posterior to the aorta before draining, commonly to the IVC
It passes anterior to the aorta in two limbs
It drains directly into the portal vein
It crosses the midline through the renal pelvis

correctAnswer.text: It passes posterior to the aorta before draining, commonly to the IVC

questions.explanation: A retro-aortic left renal vein courses behind the aorta and may enter the IVC or, in some variants, follow an abnormal caudal course to an iliac vein. The chapter depicts this as a recognized venous variant. Cross-sectional imaging is valuable for mapping its route before surgery.

questions.question: Where does renal lymphatic drainage follow the vessels to?
questions.explanation: The chapter states that renal lymphatics follow the arteries to para-aortic lymph nodes. This is anatomically consistent with the retroperitoneal location of the kidneys and is relevant when evaluating nodal disease. It differs from pelvic ureteral drainage, which includes internal and external iliac nodes.

questions.question: What is the approximate length of the ureter in the chapter?
questions.explanation: The ureter is described as connecting the renal pelvis to the bladder and measuring about 25–30 cm. Its course is retroperitoneal through the abdomen and pelvis, and it has three functionally narrow regions that are clinically important when a calculus descends from the kidney.

questions.question: Which three layers are described in the ureteric wall?

options.text: Outer cartilage, middle skeletal muscle and inner squamous epithelium
Outer adventitia, middle smooth muscle and inner transitional epithelium
Outer serosa, middle bone and inner endothelium
Outer renal cortex, middle medulla and inner urothelium

correctAnswer.text: Outer adventitia, middle smooth muscle and inner transitional epithelium

questions.explanation: The chapter describes an outer adventitia, a middle smooth-muscle layer and inner transitional cell epithelium. Smooth muscle generates peristalsis to move urine toward the bladder, while the transitional epithelium accommodates changes in luminal distension. The ureter is not simply a passive tube.

questions.question: Which is the first of the three functionally narrow regions of the ureter?

options.text: The midpoint of the bladder dome

questions.explanation: The pelviureteric junction, where the renal pelvis narrows into the ureter, is one of the three functionally narrow regions listed in the chapter. Calculi may lodge there because of the change in calibre and anatomy. The other two sites are the bony pelvic brim and the intravesical ureter.

questions.question: At which pelvic landmark is another physiological ureteric narrowing described?

options.text: At the pubic symphysis inside the bladder
Where the ureter crosses the bony pelvic brim

correctAnswer.text: Where the ureter crosses the bony pelvic brim

questions.explanation: The ureter narrows functionally where it crosses the bony pelvic brim, in addition to the pelviureteric junction and intravesical segment. These are classic locations where a descending stone may become impacted. The exact position can vary with the individual’s anatomy and vascular relationships.

questions.question: Why does the intravesical ureter act as a reflux-preventing valve?

options.text: It opens directly into the bladder dome at a right angle
It runs obliquely through the muscular bladder wall
It is closed by the renal capsule

correctAnswer.text: It runs obliquely through the muscular bladder wall

questions.explanation: The chapter explains that the intravesical ureter runs obliquely through the bladder wall, creating a valve-like mechanism that resists reflux during bladder filling and contraction. A short or incompetent intramural course can predispose to vesicoureteric reflux, as described for the lower-pole moiety in duplex systems.

questions.question: Which structure lies posterior to the abdominal ureter among the listed relations?
questions.explanation: The chapter lists the psoas muscle, genitofemoral nerve, sacroiliac joint, common iliac vessels and transverse process tips among posterior relationships along the ureter’s course. On CT, the ureter can often be traced over the psoas and near the transverse processes, especially when contrast-filled or dilated.

questions.question: Which structure is a right-sided anterior relation of the abdominal ureter listed in the chapter?
questions.explanation: The chapter lists the duodenum, gonadal vessels and colic artery among right ureter anterior relations. On the left, the gonadal and colic arteries and sigmoid mesentery are described. These relations help explain why ureteric identification can be difficult on axial imaging and during abdominal surgery.

questions.question: Which relationship between the ureter and vas deferens is described in the male pelvis?

options.text: They merge into a common duct
The ureter passes through the vas deferens
The vas deferens lies posterior to the ureter at every point
The ureter lies posterior to the vas deferens

correctAnswer.text: The ureter lies posterior to the vas deferens

questions.explanation: The chapter’s pelvic diagram states that the ureter lies anterior to the external iliac vessels and posterior to the vas deferens in the male pelvis. This relationship is relevant to pelvic surgery and to tracing the distal ureter on cross-sectional imaging.

questions.question: What is the relationship between the ureter and uterine artery in the female pelvis?

options.text: The uterine artery passes through the ureter
The ureter passes superior to the uterine artery in the broad ligament
The ureter passes inferior to the uterine artery

correctAnswer.text: The ureter passes inferior to the uterine artery

questions.explanation: The chapter notes that the ureter passes inferior to the uterine artery in the broad ligament, a classic surgical relationship often summarized as “water under the bridge.” It is clinically important during hysterectomy and other pelvic procedures because the ureter may be injured near this crossing.

questions.question: Where does the ureter deviate before entering the posterior bladder wall?

options.text: Laterally at the ischial spines, then medially
Directly across the midline without a pelvic turn

correctAnswer.text: Laterally at the ischial spines, then medially

questions.explanation: The chapter describes the ureter deviating laterally at the ischial spines before turning medially to enter the posterior bladder wall. This pelvic course is useful when tracing the distal ureter and understanding its proximity to pelvic vessels and reproductive organs.

questions.question: Which arterial supply pattern is described for the upper ureter?

options.text: Branches only from the inferior mesenteric artery
Direct supply from the portal vein
Supply exclusively from the internal pudendal artery

questions.explanation: The chapter describes the upper ureter as receiving branches from the renal artery. The mid ureter receives small medial branches from the aorta, while the lower ureter receives branches from pelvic vessels including vesical, middle rectal and uterine arteries. The segmental supply is variable, so preservation of periureteric tissue is important in surgery.

questions.question: Which spinal levels are associated with ureteric pain afferents in the chapter?
questions.explanation: The chapter states that ureteric afferent fibres travel with sympathetic nerves to spinal cord levels T12–L2. This is consistent with the typical loin-to-groin referral pattern of ureteric pain. The description concerns pain pathways; it does not imply that ureteric peristalsis depends entirely on autonomic innervation.

questions.question: How does lymphatic drainage differ between abdominal and pelvic ureter?

options.text: Abdominal ureter drains to inguinal nodes and pelvic ureter to para-aortic nodes only
Both drain exclusively to axillary nodes
Abdominal ureter drains to aortocaval/common iliac nodes; pelvic ureter to internal and external iliac nodes
Both drain directly to the portal system

correctAnswer.text: Abdominal ureter drains to aortocaval/common iliac nodes; pelvic ureter to internal and external iliac nodes

questions.explanation: The chapter distinguishes abdominal ureter drainage to aortocaval and common iliac nodes from pelvic ureter drainage to internal and external iliac nodes. This regional pattern is relevant when interpreting nodal spread and planning oncological staging. The exact drainage can overlap near the pelvic brim.

questions.question: How is the normal adrenal gland described on plain radiographs?

options.text: It is routinely outlined by periadrenal fat
Its cortex and medulla are always distinct
It is opacified during the urographic phase

questions.explanation: The chapter states that the normal adrenal gland is not seen on plain films and is also not visualized on IVU. CT and MRI usually demonstrate the glands, especially when there is sufficient retroperitoneal fat. A normal adrenal is therefore not expected to produce a distinct shadow on a plain abdominal radiograph.

questions.question: In which population is the adrenal gland more readily visible on ultrasound, according to the chapter?

options.text: Healthy adults in nearly every examination

questions.explanation: The chapter notes that the adrenal gland is easily seen in neonates because it is relatively larger, but is rarely seen on ultrasound in adults. This means that failure to identify a normal adult adrenal on ultrasound is not, by itself, abnormal. CT and MRI are generally more reliable for adrenal visualization.

questions.question: What ultrasound appearance of the adrenal gland is described in the chapter?

options.text: A bright cortical shell and no central structure
A completely calcified ring in every normal gland
A fluid-filled cavity with no internal echoes
A thin reflectile core with a transonic outer portion

correctAnswer.text: A thin reflectile core with a transonic outer portion

questions.explanation: The chapter describes a thin reflectile core and transonic outer portion on ultrasound, particularly in neonates where the gland is more readily visible. The appearance should be interpreted with age and technique in mind; adult adrenal glands are commonly difficult to visualize sonographically.

questions.question: What is the approximate pre-contrast CT appearance of a normal adrenal gland in the chapter’s imaging summary?

options.text: Isodense relative to adjacent soft tissue/liver

correctAnswer.text: Isodense relative to adjacent soft tissue/liver

questions.explanation: The chapter’s summary describes the adrenal gland as isodense before contrast and as enhancing poorly after contrast in the table. Adrenal visibility improves on CT when there is sufficient surrounding retroperitoneal fat. Characterization of a focal adrenal lesion requires more than simply recognizing the normal gland.

questions.question: Which nuclear medicine agent is described for imaging adrenal medullary disorders such as phaeochromocytoma?

options.text: Inhaled xenon as a routine adrenal tracer

questions.explanation: The chapter explains that MIBG, an analogue of guanethidine, is concentrated in sympathoadrenal tissue and can be used to image medullary disorders such as phaeochromocytoma. This is a functional imaging approach, complementing the anatomical information provided by CT and MRI.

questions.question: Why is MIBG useful for selected adrenal medullary lesions?

options.text: It concentrates in sympathoadrenal tissue and provides functional information
It measures renal length by magnification
It selectively stains the renal capsule on plain films

correctAnswer.text: It concentrates in sympathoadrenal tissue and provides functional information

questions.explanation: MIBG is taken up by sympathoadrenal tissue, allowing functional localization of certain medullary lesions. The chapter contrasts this metabolic information with conventional anatomical imaging. It is not a general-purpose contrast agent for the urinary tract and does not replace CT or MRI for all adrenal questions.

questions.question: What relationship of the adrenal glands to the kidneys is important on cross-sectional imaging?

options.text: They are located inside the renal pelvis
They lie within the bladder wall
They are intraperitoneal organs suspended from the stomach
They lie superior to the kidneys within the retroperitoneal region

correctAnswer.text: They lie superior to the kidneys within the retroperitoneal region

questions.explanation: The adrenal glands sit superomedial to the upper poles of the kidneys in the retroperitoneum, with side-specific relationships to major vessels and adjacent organs. Their small size and surrounding fat influence visibility on CT and MRI. Correct identification prevents an adrenal lesion from being confused with an upper-pole renal mass.

questions.question: What does an unenhanced CT KUB primarily help assess in urinary tract imaging?

options.text: Renal blood flow in real time
Urinary calculi and the urinary tract without intravenous contrast

correctAnswer.text: Urinary calculi and the urinary tract without intravenous contrast

questions.explanation: The chapter lists unenhanced CT KUB among the CT techniques replacing IVU and notes CT’s strength for renal calculi. Because no intravenous contrast is required to make most stones conspicuous, the study can show calculi and secondary signs of obstruction. It does not directly measure renal function or adrenal metabolic activity.

questions.question: Which phase of contrast-enhanced CT best emphasizes renal parenchymal enhancement before excreted contrast outlines the collecting system?
questions.explanation: The chapter illustrates unenhanced, corticomedullary, nephrographic and urographic CT phases. The nephrographic phase emphasizes renal parenchymal enhancement, while the urographic phase shows contrast within the collecting systems and ureters. Matching the acquisition phase to the clinical question improves anatomical interpretation.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of the urographic phase in CT urography?

options.text: To opacify the collecting systems and ureters with excreted contrast
To show only the renal arteries before contrast arrival
To remove the renal parenchyma from the image

correctAnswer.text: To opacify the collecting systems and ureters with excreted contrast

questions.explanation: During the urographic phase, contrast excreted into urine outlines the renal pelvis, calyces and ureters. This phase is useful for evaluating urinary tract anatomy and filling defects. Earlier phases answer different questions, including vascular and parenchymal assessment, so CT urography often uses a multiphase strategy.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a corticomedullary CT phase?

options.text: To visualize the adrenal glands using MIBG
To show only the bladder after micturition
To emphasize differential enhancement of renal cortex and medulla and vascular anatomy

correctAnswer.text: To emphasize differential enhancement of renal cortex and medulla and vascular anatomy

questions.explanation: The corticomedullary phase occurs early after contrast injection and accentuates the cortex and renal vasculature relative to the medulla. The chapter’s multiphase CT figure distinguishes it from the nephrographic and urographic phases. It can therefore be valuable when the question concerns renal perfusion or vascular anatomy.

questions.question: Which renal contour feature is shown in the chapter as a normal variant on CT?

options.text: A renal pelvis opening into the adrenal gland
A duplicated urinary bladder in all adults
A splenic (dromedary) hump of the left kidney
A horseshoe isthmus in every normal kidney

correctAnswer.text: A splenic (dromedary) hump of the left kidney

questions.explanation: The chapter’s vascular-anomaly montage labels a splenic or dromedary hump of the left kidney. This is a contour prominence related to the adjacent spleen and can mimic a renal mass if the normal contour is unfamiliar. Its continuity with normal renal parenchyma on cross-sectional imaging helps establish the variant.

questions.question: What is the main radiological clue that a dromedary hump is a normal contour variant rather than a renal mass?

options.text: It follows the contour of otherwise normal renal parenchyma and has matching tissue characteristics
It is separated from the kidney by a capsule
It enhances exactly like the bladder lumen

correctAnswer.text: It follows the contour of otherwise normal renal parenchyma and has matching tissue characteristics

questions.explanation: A dromedary hump is a normal focal prominence of the renal contour, classically on the left adjacent to the spleen. Demonstrating that it has the same parenchymal enhancement and signal as the rest of the kidney supports a normal variant. A true mass more often distorts the contour or differs in enhancement or signal.

questions.question: What should be considered when planning renal surgery in a patient with an ectopic kidney?

options.text: An aberrant arterial supply may be present and should be mapped
The kidney never has a blood supply
The ureter always crosses into the opposite bladder wall
The adrenal gland necessarily replaces the renal parenchyma

correctAnswer.text: An aberrant arterial supply may be present and should be mapped

questions.explanation: The chapter notes that ectopic and fused kidneys commonly have aberrant vascular supply. Because vessels may arise from the aorta or iliac arteries at unusual levels, preoperative vascular mapping is important. Assuming standard hilar vessels can lead to missed branches or inadvertent injury.

questions.question: Which renal fusion anomaly is described as very rare, with both kidneys pelvic and fused?
questions.explanation: The chapter’s table describes a pancake or discoid kidney as a very rare configuration in which both kidneys are pelvic and fused. It differs from a horseshoe kidney, where the lower poles are fused but renal tissue remains on either side of the midline. Such extensive fusion can be accompanied by atypical vessels and collecting-system anatomy.

questions.question: What is the main anatomical difference between a horseshoe kidney and a pancake kidney?

options.text: A pancake kidney is always a normal single kidney
A horseshoe kidney has no renal tissue
A horseshoe kidney has fused lower poles; a pancake kidney is a more complete fused pelvic mass
A pancake kidney is defined by duplicated adrenal glands

correctAnswer.text: A horseshoe kidney has fused lower poles; a pancake kidney is a more complete fused pelvic mass

questions.explanation: The chapter describes horseshoe kidney as fusion of the lower poles, whereas a pancake/discoid kidney is a rare fusion of both kidneys in a pelvic location. This difference affects the overall shape, position and likely vascular anatomy, so the terms should not be used interchangeably.

questions.question: Which anomaly is associated with failure of renal migration rather than fusion of the lower poles?
questions.explanation: A pelvic kidney results from failure of normal ascent. Horseshoe and pancake kidneys are fusion anomalies, while a circumaortic renal vein is a venous variant. Separating positional, fusion and vascular anomalies makes the imaging description more precise.

questions.question: Which collecting-system abnormality is more likely to be associated with a duplex upper-pole moiety?
questions.explanation: The chapter notes that the upper-pole moiety in a duplex system may obstruct or have a ureterocele because its ureter tends to insert ectopically and more caudally. The lower-pole moiety, by contrast, tends to reflux. This pattern helps explain why the two moieties can have different imaging appearances and complications.

questions.question: What does the chapter say about the frequency of bilateral duplex kidney/ureter?
questions.explanation: The chapter’s table reports that duplex kidney and ureter are bilateral in about 20% of cases and more common in females than males. These figures are epidemiological estimates; the important radiological task is to determine whether duplication is complete or partial and to trace the drainage of each moiety.

questions.question: What sex ratio is given for duplex kidney and ureter in the chapter?
questions.explanation: The chapter’s table gives a female-to-male ratio of approximately 2:1 for duplex kidney and ureter. This is a population-level observation, not a diagnostic criterion. Imaging diagnosis depends on demonstrating duplicated collecting-system anatomy and assessing associated obstruction or reflux-related changes.

questions.question: Which statement about the renal vein tributaries is most accurate according to the chapter?

options.text: Renal venous branches are end arteries with no communication
Venous channels and branch renal veins communicate, but ultimately drain to the main renal vein
All renal venous blood drains through the portal vein
Renal veins normally drain into the ureter

correctAnswer.text: Venous channels and branch renal veins communicate, but ultimately drain to the main renal vein

questions.explanation: The chapter notes that renal venules and branch renal veins freely communicate throughout the parenchyma, ultimately draining to the main renal vein. This contrasts with the end-arterial nature of segmental arterial supply. The distinction helps explain why arterial occlusion can cause segmental infarction despite a more interconnected venous network.

questions.question: Which statement about the right renal vein is supported by the chapter?

options.text: It is short, about 2–4 cm, and has few major tributaries compared with the left renal vein
It is three times longer than the left renal vein
It normally receives the left gonadal and left adrenal veins
It routinely passes behind the aorta in two limbs

correctAnswer.text: It is short, about 2–4 cm, and has few major tributaries compared with the left renal vein

questions.explanation: The chapter describes the right renal vein as about 2–4 cm long and contrasts it with the longer left renal vein. The left vein receives the left adrenal and gonadal tributaries, while the right renal vein typically drains directly into the IVC. These differences matter in surgical and vascular imaging.

questions.question: What is the typical lymphatic drainage route of the kidney according to the chapter?

options.text: Along the ureter directly to superficial inguinal nodes only
Along renal arteries toward para-aortic nodes

correctAnswer.text: Along renal arteries toward para-aortic nodes

questions.explanation: Renal lymphatics follow the arterial supply to para-aortic nodes. This expected pathway is useful when assessing retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy in patients with renal malignancy or inflammatory disease. It is distinct from drainage of the lower urinary tract, which follows pelvic lymphatic pathways.

questions.question: Why can the renal outline be visible on plain radiographs even though the renal parenchyma cannot be resolved?

options.text: The cortex is radiopaque like bone
Perirenal fat can create a contrast boundary around the organ
The renal artery outlines every nephron

correctAnswer.text: Perirenal fat can create a contrast boundary around the organ

questions.explanation: The chapter explains that surrounding perirenal fat may outline the renal edge on plain films, but intrarenal anatomy is never visible. The radiograph can therefore provide limited information about gross position or size, not direct assessment of cortex, medulla or calyces.

questions.question: What limitation of ultrasound for adult adrenal assessment is stated in the chapter?

options.text: The normal adrenal is always the brightest abdominal organ
The normal adrenal is rarely visualized in adults
Ultrasound cannot depict the neonatal adrenal
Ultrasound routinely shows adrenal microanatomy better than MRI

correctAnswer.text: The normal adrenal is rarely visualized in adults

questions.explanation: Although ultrasound can show the adrenal gland in neonates, the chapter says it is rarely seen in adults. Surrounding bowel gas, body habitus and the small size of the normal gland limit visualization. CT and MRI are therefore more dependable for assessing adrenal anatomy in adults.

questions.question: Which modality is described as the first-line test for assessment of the male genitourinary tract?
questions.explanation: The chapter identifies ultrasound as the first-line modality for the male genitourinary tract. It avoids ionizing radiation and can assess the bladder, prostate, testes and penis with technique selected for the organ of interest. Choose the examination according to the clinical question: ultrasound avoids ionizing radiation, MRI offers superior soft-tissue contrast, and CT remains particularly valuable in trauma.

questions.question: For transabdominal ultrasound of the bladder, what preparation improves the acoustic window?

options.text: An empty bladder after immediate micturition

questions.explanation: A distended bladder acts as an acoustic window for transabdominal ultrasound. Filling also helps define the bladder contour and wall; interpretation of wall thickness must account for the degree of distension. Choose the examination according to the clinical question: ultrasound avoids ionizing radiation, MRI offers superior soft-tissue contrast, and CT remains particularly valuable in trauma.

questions.question: Why is CT generally not the first-line test for routine male pelvic soft-tissue disorders?

options.text: It uses ionizing radiation and has lower soft-tissue contrast resolution than MRI
It is incapable of multiplanar reconstruction

correctAnswer.text: It uses ionizing radiation and has lower soft-tissue contrast resolution than MRI

questions.explanation: The chapter cautions against CT as a first-line examination because the testes are radiosensitive and CT has lower contrast resolution than MRI for structures such as the prostate and penis. CT remains valuable when rapid assessment is needed, especially in trauma. Choose the examination according to the clinical question: ultrasound avoids ionizing radiation, MRI offers superior soft-tissue contrast, and CT remains particularly valuable in trauma.

questions.question: In the chapter, which modality is best for demonstrating male pelvic soft tissues overall?
questions.explanation: MRI offers superior contrast resolution and multiplanar imaging and is described as demonstrating male pelvic soft tissues better than other modalities. The chapter distinguishes T1-weighted imaging for anatomy from T2-weighted imaging for pathology. Choose the examination according to the clinical question: ultrasound avoids ionizing radiation, MRI offers superior soft-tissue contrast, and CT remains particularly valuable in trauma.

questions.question: Which MRI weighting is described as best for defining anatomy in the male pelvis?
questions.explanation: The chapter states that T1-weighted images are best for defining anatomy, whereas T2-weighted images are best for evaluating pathology. The two are complementary rather than interchangeable. Choose the examination according to the clinical question: ultrasound avoids ionizing radiation, MRI offers superior soft-tissue contrast, and CT remains particularly valuable in trauma.

questions.question: What remains the gold-standard technique for delineating the internal iliac arterial tree according to the chapter?
questions.explanation: Colour and pulsed-wave Doppler ultrasound, CT angiography and MR angiography can assess pelvic vessels. The chapter nevertheless identifies invasive pelvic angiography as the gold standard, particularly for detailed depiction of the internal iliac arterial tree. Choose the examination according to the clinical question: ultrasound avoids ionizing radiation, MRI offers superior soft-tissue contrast, and CT remains particularly valuable in trauma.

questions.question: What is the principal function of the pelvic floor?
questions.explanation: The pelvic floor is a sling of muscle and fascia supporting pelvic viscera. It is pierced anteriorly by the urethra and posteriorly by the rectum, making its anatomy important in pelvic support and perineal relationships. Orient these structures in relation to the ischial tuberosities, pubic arch, coccyx and perineal membrane; those landmarks define the compartments on anatomical diagrams and cross-sectional imaging.

questions.question: Which line divides the perineum into urogenital and anal triangles?

options.text: A line joining the anterior superior iliac spines
A line joining the ischial tuberosities
A line between the pubic symphysis and coccyx
A line joining the femoral heads

correctAnswer.text: A line joining the ischial tuberosities

questions.explanation: A line drawn between the ischial tuberosities separates the anterior urogenital triangle from the posterior anal triangle. This is a surface-anatomical division of the perineum, not a division of the pelvic cavity. Orient these structures in relation to the ischial tuberosities, pubic arch, coccyx and perineal membrane; those landmarks define the compartments on anatomical diagrams and cross-sectional imaging.

questions.question: Which structure forms the anterior boundary of the perineum?
questions.explanation: The chapter table lists the pubic symphysis as the anterior boundary and the coccyx as the posterior boundary. The ischiopubic rami and ischial tuberosities form the anterolateral boundaries, while sacrotuberous ligaments form the posterolateral boundaries. Orient these structures in relation to the ischial tuberosities, pubic arch, coccyx and perineal membrane; those landmarks define the compartments on anatomical diagrams and cross-sectional imaging.

questions.question: Which structure forms the posterior boundary of the perineum?
questions.explanation: The coccyx marks the posterior boundary of the perineum in the chapter’s boundary table. The distinction is useful when orienting sagittal and axial pelvic images and understanding the extent of the perineal region. Orient these structures in relation to the ischial tuberosities, pubic arch, coccyx and perineal membrane; those landmarks define the compartments on anatomical diagrams and cross-sectional imaging.

questions.question: Which structure is a content of the male deep perineal pouch?
questions.explanation: The deep perineal pouch lies above the perineal membrane and below the pelvic-floor fascia. Its male contents include the deep transverse perineal muscles, voluntary external urethral sphincter and paired bulbourethral glands. Orient these structures in relation to the ischial tuberosities, pubic arch, coccyx and perineal membrane; those landmarks define the compartments on anatomical diagrams and cross-sectional imaging.

questions.question: Where do the ducts of the bulbourethral (Cowper) glands open?
questions.explanation: The bulbourethral glands lie in the deep perineal region, and their ducts open into the bulbar urethra about 2.5 cm below the perineal membrane. This location distinguishes them from the prostatic ducts and ejaculatory ducts, which open into the prostatic urethra. Orient these structures in relation to the ischial tuberosities, pubic arch, coccyx and perineal membrane; those landmarks define the compartments on anatomical diagrams and cross-sectional imaging.

questions.question: Where is the bladder trigone located?

options.text: At the base of the bladder, between the ureteric orifices and internal urethral orifice
At the bladder dome between the urachus and median umbilical ligament
Within the prostate around the prostatic urethra
At the junction of bladder and ureter outside the wall

correctAnswer.text: At the base of the bladder, between the ureteric orifices and internal urethral orifice

questions.explanation: The trigone is a triangular region at the bladder base. Its two superolateral corners are the ureteric orifices and its inferomedial corner is the internal urethral orifice; unlike much of the bladder lining, it remains smooth when the bladder is distended. For interpretation, correlate the finding with bladder filling and the relationships of the bladder base to the ureters, prostate, seminal vesicles and rectum.

questions.question: How does the bladder typically change shape as it fills?

options.text: It becomes triangular and descends into the perineum
It remains fixed entirely within the pelvis
It becomes flattened against the sacrum
It becomes ovoid and its superior surface rises extraperitoneally into the abdomen

correctAnswer.text: It becomes ovoid and its superior surface rises extraperitoneally into the abdomen

questions.explanation: As the bladder fills, it becomes ovoid and its superior surface rises into the abdomen while remaining extraperitoneal. This change affects its relations and the appearance of the wall on imaging. For interpretation, correlate the finding with bladder filling and the relationships of the bladder base to the ureters, prostate, seminal vesicles and rectum.

questions.question: Which description of bladder wall appearance is correct?

options.text: It is always equally thick and smooth regardless of filling
It is smooth only when collapsed and trabeculated when full
It is thick and trabeculated when collapsed, and thinner and smoother when distended
The trigone becomes prominently trabeculated during filling

correctAnswer.text: It is thick and trabeculated when collapsed, and thinner and smoother when distended

questions.explanation: The apparent bladder wall depends on distension: a collapsed bladder has a thicker, trabeculated appearance, while a distended bladder wall appears thinner and smoother. The trigone remains smooth, so wall thickness should be assessed with the bladder state in mind. For interpretation, correlate the finding with bladder filling and the relationships of the bladder base to the ureters, prostate, seminal vesicles and rectum.

questions.question: The vesical venous plexus drains primarily into which veins?
questions.explanation: Venous drainage from the bladder passes through the vesical plexus into the internal iliac veins. This local pelvic drainage pattern is separate from portal venous drainage of the gastrointestinal tract. For interpretation, correlate the finding with bladder filling and the relationships of the bladder base to the ureters, prostate, seminal vesicles and rectum.

questions.question: What lymphatic drainage pathway is described for the bladder?

options.text: Internal iliac nodes, then para-aortic nodes
Directly to the thoracic duct without nodal stations

correctAnswer.text: Internal iliac nodes, then para-aortic nodes

questions.explanation: The chapter lists drainage to internal iliac and then para-aortic lymph nodes. Knowing the described pathway provides a framework for understanding pelvic nodal assessment, while actual drainage can vary with the region involved. For interpretation, correlate the finding with bladder filling and the relationships of the bladder base to the ureters, prostate, seminal vesicles and rectum.

questions.question: What is the chapter’s ultrasound reference for normal bladder wall thickness?

options.text: It should always be greater than 10 mm
It is fixed at exactly 1 mm
It cannot be assessed by ultrasound
It should not exceed about 3–5 mm, depending on distension

correctAnswer.text: It should not exceed about 3–5 mm, depending on distension

questions.explanation: The chapter notes a wall thickness of no more than approximately 3–5 mm, depending on how distended the bladder is. Because an underfilled bladder may look falsely thick, measurement must be interpreted in relation to filling. For interpretation, correlate the finding with bladder filling and the relationships of the bladder base to the ureters, prostate, seminal vesicles and rectum.

questions.question: How can the bladder be filled with contrast for imaging?

options.text: Only by direct puncture of the bladder wall
Antegradely during intravenous urography or retrogradely through the urethra for cystography
Only by injecting contrast into the renal artery

correctAnswer.text: Antegradely during intravenous urography or retrogradely through the urethra for cystography

questions.explanation: The chapter describes contrast filling during intravenous urography and retrograde filling through the urethra for cystography. A normally full bladder has a smooth regular outline; after micturition, corrugations may be visible. For interpretation, correlate the finding with bladder filling and the relationships of the bladder base to the ureters, prostate, seminal vesicles and rectum.

questions.question: Which modality is described as most useful for evaluating the bladder wall?
questions.explanation: CT and MRI can demonstrate the bladder’s relationships to surrounding structures, but the chapter specifically notes MRI as most useful for evaluating the bladder wall. Ultrasound is also useful for direct wall assessment and dynamic evaluation. For interpretation, correlate the finding with bladder filling and the relationships of the bladder base to the ureters, prostate, seminal vesicles and rectum.

questions.question: What developmental failure is given as the cause of bladder agenesis?

options.text: Failure of the cloaca to divide into anterior bladder and posterior rectum
Failure of the ureteric bud to contact metanephric tissue only
Failure of the Müllerian ducts to regress

correctAnswer.text: Failure of the cloaca to divide into anterior bladder and posterior rectum

questions.explanation: The chapter describes bladder agenesis as a rare anomaly caused by failure of the cloaca to divide into an anterior bladder and posterior rectum. This is a developmental partitioning problem rather than an acquired bladder-wall abnormality. For interpretation, correlate the finding with bladder filling and the relationships of the bladder base to the ureters, prostate, seminal vesicles and rectum.

questions.question: What is bladder septation?

options.text: Cystic dilatation of the terminal ureter
Two completely separate bladders with separate urethras
A tear in the bladder dome after trauma
Division of one bladder into two portions by a sagittal or coronal septum

correctAnswer.text: Division of one bladder into two portions by a sagittal or coronal septum

questions.explanation: Bladder septation refers to a single bladder divided into two portions by a septum in the sagittal or coronal plane. It is distinct from complete duplication, in which two separate bladder cavities and separate urethras are described. For interpretation, correlate the finding with bladder filling and the relationships of the bladder base to the ureters, prostate, seminal vesicles and rectum.

questions.question: What is a ureterocoele?

options.text: A congenital septum dividing the bladder
A diverticulum arising from the penile urethra
Cystic dilatation of the terminal intravesical ureter
A cyst in the midline prostate derived from Müllerian ducts

correctAnswer.text: Cystic dilatation of the terminal intravesical ureter

questions.explanation: A ureterocoele is a cystic dilatation of the distal ureter within the bladder. On intravenous urogram, the chapter illustrates a rounded distal ureteral dilatation with a thin surrounding lucent line, producing the “cobra head” appearance. For interpretation, correlate the finding with bladder filling and the relationships of the bladder base to the ureters, prostate, seminal vesicles and rectum.

questions.question: Why can pelvic fractures be associated with bladder rupture?

options.text: The bladder is entirely intraperitoneal and freely mobile
The bladder neck is relatively fixed to the pelvis
The ureters attach directly to the pubic symphysis
The bladder has no fascial attachments

correctAnswer.text: The bladder neck is relatively fixed to the pelvis

questions.explanation: The chapter links bladder rupture in pelvic trauma to the relatively fixed bladder neck. The pattern of contrast extravasation on cystography helps distinguish extraperitoneal from intraperitoneal injury. For interpretation, correlate the finding with bladder filling and the relationships of the bladder base to the ureters, prostate, seminal vesicles and rectum.

questions.question: What proportion of major bladder injuries are described as extraperitoneal?
questions.explanation: The chapter states that extraperitoneal rupture accounts for approximately 80–90% of major bladder injuries. It is commonly associated with penetrating trauma in the chapter’s description, and cystography can show variable paths of extravasated contrast. For interpretation, correlate the finding with bladder filling and the relationships of the bladder base to the ureters, prostate, seminal vesicles and rectum.

questions.question: What is the typical mechanism of intraperitoneal bladder rupture described in the chapter?

options.text: A chronic low-grade obstruction of the prostatic ducts
A congenital absence of the trigone
A ureterocoele emptying into the bladder
A direct blow to an already distended bladder

correctAnswer.text: A direct blow to an already distended bladder

questions.explanation: Intraperitoneal rupture is described as approximately 10–20% of bladder injuries and typically follows a direct blow to a distended bladder. Contrast may spread into the peritoneal cavity, around bowel loops, between mesenteric folds and into paracolic gutters. For interpretation, correlate the finding with bladder filling and the relationships of the bladder base to the ureters, prostate, seminal vesicles and rectum.

questions.question: Approximately how long is the male urethra?
questions.explanation: The chapter gives an overall male urethral length of approximately 18–20 cm. It is divided into posterior prostatic and membranous portions and anterior bulbar and penile portions, each with distinct anatomical relationships. For urethral imaging, first localize the finding to the posterior or anterior segment, because the surrounding structures and the contrast technique used to demonstrate each segment differ.

questions.question: Which portions make up the posterior male urethra?

options.text: Navicular fossa and external meatus only

questions.explanation: The posterior urethra consists of the prostatic and membranous portions, while the anterior urethra consists of bulbar and penile portions. This division is clinically relevant when interpreting contrast urethrography and locating congenital obstruction. For urethral imaging, first localize the finding to the posterior or anterior segment, because the surrounding structures and the contrast technique used to demonstrate each segment differ.

questions.question: What is the approximate length of the prostatic urethra?
questions.explanation: The prostatic urethra is approximately 3–4 cm long and passes through the prostate from the bladder neck. The membranous portion is much shorter, about 1.5 cm, and traverses the external urethral sphincter. For urethral imaging, first localize the finding to the posterior or anterior segment, because the surrounding structures and the contrast technique used to demonstrate each segment differ.

questions.question: Where do the prostatic ducts open?

options.text: Into the membranous urethra distal to the sphincter
Into the prostatic sinuses on either side of the urethral crest

correctAnswer.text: Into the prostatic sinuses on either side of the urethral crest

options.text: Both open into the bladder trigone
The prostatic sinuses lie in the navicular fossa
Prostatic sinuses receive multiple prostatic ducts on either side of the urethral crest; ejaculatory ducts open beside the utricle at the verumontanum
The ejaculatory ducts open into the bulbar urethra

correctAnswer.text: Prostatic sinuses receive multiple prostatic ducts on either side of the urethral crest; ejaculatory ducts open beside the utricle at the verumontanum

questions.explanation: The prostatic sinuses are shallow depressions on either side of the urethral crest and receive around 15–20 prostatic ducts. The ejaculatory ducts instead open into the prostatic urethra on either side of the prostatic utricle at the verumontanum. Trace the reproductive pathway in order from epididymis through vas deferens, ejaculatory duct and prostatic urethra; this avoids confusing it with the urinary drainage pathway.

questions.question: Which structures form the crura of the penis?

options.text: The distal ends of the corpus spongiosum
The paired corpora cavernosa as they diverge posterosuperiorly

correctAnswer.text: The paired corpora cavernosa as they diverge posterosuperiorly

questions.explanation: The corpora cavernosa fuse in the median plane within the body of the penis but diverge posterosuperiorly to form the crura. The corpus spongiosum instead expands into the bulb proximally and the glans distally. The three erectile bodies have different positions and relationships, so naming the exact body is important when describing penile anatomy or an imaging finding.

questions.question: Which structure is penetrated by the bulbar urethra in its posterior part?
questions.explanation: The proximal expansion of the corpus spongiosum forms the bulb, and its posterior part is penetrated by the bulbar urethra. The urethra then continues distally within the corpus spongiosum to the external meatus. The three erectile bodies have different positions and relationships, so naming the exact body is important when describing penile anatomy or an imaging finding.

questions.question: Which tissue feature helps explain why the erectile bodies enhance strongly after contrast administration?

options.text: The corpora contain no blood vessels
The corpora are made entirely of fat
The corpora are continuous with the bladder lumen

questions.explanation: The chapter notes that the corpora are very vascular on contrast-enhanced images. This is consistent with their erectile function, in which arterial inflow and distension of sinusoidal spaces alter venous outflow and produce erection. The three erectile bodies have different positions and relationships, so naming the exact body is important when describing penile anatomy or an imaging finding.

questions.question: A congenital midline cyst in the prostate extends toward the base along the embryological course of the Müllerian ducts. Which diagnosis best matches the chapter?
questions.explanation: The chapter describes a Müllerian duct cyst as a congenital midline prostatic cyst derived from the Müllerian ducts, often large and extending toward the prostate base. A ureterocoele, in contrast, is a cystic dilatation of the terminal intravesical ureter. The anatomical level of the abnormality helps explain its consequences: a posterior urethral obstruction may affect the bladder and upper urinary tract, whereas penile anomalies affect distal anatomy.

questions.question: Which penile congenital anomaly is described as ventral or rotational curvature most evident during erection?
questions.explanation: Chordee is the curvature described in the chapter, caused by fibrous tissue along the course of the corpus spongiosum. It is often associated with hypospadias and becomes more apparent during erection. The anatomical level of the abnormality helps explain its consequences: a posterior urethral obstruction may affect the bladder and upper urinary tract, whereas penile anomalies affect distal anatomy.

questions.question: Which of the following is listed among less common penile anomalies?
questions.explanation: The chapter lists penile agenesis, duplication and lymphoedema as less common anomalies, and separately describes chordee and microphallus. Ureterocoele and bladder agenesis are urinary tract anomalies rather than penile anomalies. The anatomical level of the abnormality helps explain its consequences: a posterior urethral obstruction may affect the bladder and upper urinary tract, whereas penile anomalies affect distal anatomy.

questions.question: Which bladder injury pattern is more common in major bladder trauma according to the chapter?
questions.explanation: Extraperitoneal rupture accounts for approximately 80–90% of major bladder injuries in the chapter. The distinction from intraperitoneal rupture matters because the distribution of contrast on cystography differs, with intraperitoneal contrast outlining bowel loops and tracking along peritoneal recesses. The distribution of extravasated contrast is the key imaging clue: intraperitoneal leakage tracks around bowel and peritoneal recesses, whereas extraperitoneal leakage tends to remain around the pelvis.

questions.question: Which paired structure contributes about 60% of seminal fluid and lies posterior to the bladder?
questions.explanation: The seminal vesicles are paired lobulated sacs near the bladder base, posterior to the bladder and above the prostate. They contribute about 60% of seminal fluid, whereas the prostate contributes about 30% according to the chapter. The relationship is best understood in three dimensions by combining the named structure with adjacent organs and the relevant pelvic compartment, rather than memorizing the term in isolation.

questions.question: Which of the following is a correct pairing of structure and modality emphasized in the chapter?

options.text: Bladder wall — plain AP radiography as best test

questions.explanation: The chapter recommends high-frequency linear ultrasound for the testes and penis. MRI is preferred for male pelvic soft tissues and prostate zonal anatomy, while Doppler ultrasound can assess penile arterial flow and bladder ultrasound can assess wall thickness and ureteric jets. The relationship is best understood in three dimensions by combining the named structure with adjacent organs and the relevant pelvic compartment, rather than memorizing the term in isolation.

questions.question: Which statement about MRI of the penis is consistent with the chapter?

options.text: Appearance varies with sequence and state of erection
The corpora always have identical signal on every sequence
The fascial layers are high signal on T2 while corpora are low signal
MRI cannot demonstrate the root of the penis

correctAnswer.text: Appearance varies with sequence and state of erection

questions.explanation: The chapter notes that penile MRI appearances vary according to sequence and the state of erection. T1-weighted images show the corpora at signal lower than fat and higher than muscle, while T2-weighted images show increased signal in the corpora relative to the fascial layers. The relationship is best understood in three dimensions by combining the named structure with adjacent organs and the relevant pelvic compartment, rather than memorizing the term in isolation.

questions.question: Which structure lies between the bladder and rectum at the base of the bladder, with seminal vesicles and vas deferens contributing to the lower relationship?

options.text: The rectovesical region/pouch separates the bladder base from the rectum superiorly

correctAnswer.text: The rectovesical region/pouch separates the bladder base from the rectum superiorly

questions.explanation: The bladder base is separated from the rectum by the rectovesical pouch above and by the seminal vesicles and vas deferens below. This layered relationship helps explain why bladder, seminal vesicle, prostate and rectal anatomy must be interpreted together on pelvic cross-sectional imaging. The relationship is best understood in three dimensions by combining the named structure with adjacent organs and the relevant pelvic compartment, rather than memorizing the term in isolation.

questions.question: Which anatomical feature is useful for distinguishing bladder trigone from much of the rest of the bladder wall?

options.text: The trigone is the only part covered by peritoneum
The trigone contains the prostatic sinuses
The trigone remains smooth even when the bladder is distended
The trigone lies in the penile corpus spongiosum

correctAnswer.text: The trigone remains smooth even when the bladder is distended

questions.explanation: The chapter notes that the trigone remains smooth while the rest of the bladder wall changes with distension. Its boundaries are the ureteric orifices and internal urethral orifice, making it a defined region at the bladder base. The relationship is best understood in three dimensions by combining the named structure with adjacent organs and the relevant pelvic compartment, rather than memorizing the term in isolation.

questions.question: Which of the following correctly matches an anatomical region with its contents?

options.text: Deep perineal pouch — prostate and seminal vesicles
Male urogenital triangle — penis and scrotum

correctAnswer.text: Male urogenital triangle — penis and scrotum

questions.explanation: The male urogenital triangle is the anterior part of the perineum and contains the penis and scrotum. The deep perineal pouch contains the external urethral sphincter, deep transverse perineal muscles and bulbourethral glands, while the trigone and prostatic sinuses are urinary tract landmarks. The relationship is best understood in three dimensions by combining the named structure with adjacent organs and the relevant pelvic compartment, rather than memorizing the term in isolation.

questions.question: Which plane defines the inlet of the true pelvis?

options.text: A plane through the ischial tuberosities and coccyx only
A plane through the femoral heads
A horizontal plane through the iliac crests
A plane passing through the sacral promontory, arcuate line, iliopectineal line and posterior pubic crest

correctAnswer.text: A plane passing through the sacral promontory, arcuate line, iliopectineal line and posterior pubic crest

questions.explanation: The pelvic inlet is defined by the bony brim: posteriorly the sacral promontory, laterally the arcuate line of the ilium and iliopectineal line, and anteriorly the posterior surface of the pubic crest. This boundary separates the greater (false) pelvis above from the true pelvis below, which contains the pelvic viscera. The outlet is a different, more inferior plane.

questions.question: Which pelvic type is described as the common normal female type, with a slightly transverse-oval inlet and a subpubic angle of about 90–100°?
questions.explanation: The gynaecoid pelvis is described as the usual female pattern. Its inlet is slightly transversely oval, the sacrum has average concavity and inclination, the side walls are relatively straight, the ischial spines are blunt, and the subpubic angle is approximately 90–100°. The other named types differ in inlet shape, diameter proportions and side-wall configuration.

questions.question: A pelvis with long anteroposterior diameters, short transverse diameters and a long narrow sacrum is which type?
questions.explanation: The anthropoid pelvis has relatively long anteroposterior diameters and short transverse diameters, with a long narrow sacrum. The sacrosciatic notch is described as wide, while the subpubic angle is narrow. This differs from the gynaecoid pattern, whose inlet is slightly transverse oval, and from the platypelloid pattern, which is broad transversely but shallow anteroposteriorly.

questions.question: Which pelvic type has short anteroposterior diameters and long transverse diameters?
questions.explanation: The platypelloid pelvis is the flat type: the anteroposterior diameters are short and the transverse diameters are long. The chapter also describes a wide subpubic angle and a narrow sacrosciatic notch. The anthropoid pelvis has the opposite diameter emphasis, with long anteroposterior dimensions and short transverse dimensions.

questions.question: Which muscles are listed as forming the posterior pelvic wall?
questions.explanation: The chapter identifies psoas and iliacus as the muscles forming the posterior pelvic wall. On cross-sectional imaging, these muscles lie along the anterolateral lumbar spine and iliac fossa and are useful landmarks for the pelvic brim and iliac vessels. The abdominal wall muscles are instead associated with the anterior wall.

questions.question: Which structure forms the inferior boundary of the pelvic floor in the chapter's boundary list?
questions.explanation: The chapter lists the pelvic diaphragm as the inferior boundary in its description of the pelvic floor. The anterior boundary includes the symphysis pubis and pubic bodies; lateral boundaries include the ilium, ischium, piriformis and obturator internus; posterior boundaries include the sacrum, coccyx, piriformis and coccygeus. These relationships help orient MRI sections of the pelvic floor.

questions.question: Which two regions divide the perineum in the chapter's diagram?

options.text: Right and left ischioanal compartments only

questions.explanation: The perineum is divided into the urogenital triangle anteriorly and the anal triangle posteriorly. The urogenital triangle contains the external genital structures and urethral and vaginal openings, while the anal triangle contains the anal canal and anal sphincters. This division is an important surface-anatomy framework for understanding pelvic-floor imaging and perineal spaces.

questions.question: What separates the two parts of the urogenital triangle described in the chapter?
questions.explanation: The perineal membrane is a triangular sheet stretching horizontally across the deep perineal pouch and divides the urogenital triangle into two parts. It attaches laterally to the ischiopubic rami, with its apex at the arcuate ligament of the pubis, and fuses posteriorly with the deep part of the perineal body. The chapter notes that it is less well defined in females.

questions.question: The superficial perineal space is enclosed by which fascial layers?

options.text: Rectus sheath and transversalis fascia only

questions.explanation: The chapter describes the superficial perineal space as enclosed by fatty and membranous (Colles') fascia. Colles' fascia attaches posteriorly to the posterior border of the perineal membrane and laterally to the pubic arch; anteriorly it continues with Scarpa's fascia of the anterior abdominal wall and over the clitoris. These fascial continuities help explain the anatomical spread of fluid in the superficial perineum.

questions.question: Which artery enters the deep perineal pouch on each side and gives off arteries to the clitoris?
questions.explanation: The internal pudendal artery enters the deep perineal pouch on each side and gives branches to the clitoris. The chapter describes it in relation to the deep perineal space and the perineal membrane. The ovarian artery supplies the ovary and tube, while the inferior mesenteric artery supplies hindgut structures, so neither is the relevant perineal vessel.

questions.question: What is found in the vaginal vestibule?

options.text: Vaginal and urethral orifices and openings of the greater vestibular glands

correctAnswer.text: Vaginal and urethral orifices and openings of the greater vestibular glands

questions.explanation: The vestibule is the space between the labia minora. It contains the vaginal and urethral orifices and the openings of the greater vestibular (Bartholin) glands. The cervical canal and uterine ostia are internal structures, while the bladder trigone lies inside the urinary bladder.

questions.question: Which nodal groups receive lymph from the vulva according to the chapter?
questions.explanation: The chapter lists superficial and deep inguinal nodes for vulval lymphatic drainage. This is clinically important because vulval disease may spread to inguinal nodal groups, which can be assessed by ultrasound, CT or MRI depending on the clinical setting. Para-aortic nodes are more closely associated with ovarian drainage.

questions.question: What is the approximate length of the vagina given in the chapter?
questions.explanation: The vagina is described as a fibromuscular tube approximately 7–9 cm long, ascending up and back from the vestibule to surround the cervix. The posterior wall is about 1 cm longer than the anterior wall, and the upper end forms fornices around the cervix. Length and orientation are useful when interpreting sagittal pelvic MRI and planning procedures.

questions.question: Which vaginal fornix is the deepest and related to the rectouterine pouch?
questions.explanation: The posterior fornix is the deepest recess around the cervix and is related to the rectouterine pouch (pouch of Douglas). This relationship is important on sagittal imaging because the pouch lies between the posterior uterus and anterior rectum and may contain free fluid.
