questions.question: Which feature is a key reason for reviewing the axillary nerve after a proximal humeral fracture?

options.text: It passes through the carpal tunnel
It courses around the surgical neck of the humerus
It runs behind the medial epicondyle

correctAnswer.text: It courses around the surgical neck of the humerus

questions.explanation: The axillary nerve wraps around the surgical neck of the humerus, so fracture displacement may place it at risk. This differs from the ulnar nerve behind the medial epicondyle and the median nerve at the carpal tunnel, allowing the level of injury to guide clinical assessment.

questions.question: Which statement about the radius during supination is correct?

options.text: The radius rotates around the humerus only
The radius and ulna lie relatively parallel
The radius becomes the medial forearm bone in anatomical position
The radius crosses the ulna maximally

correctAnswer.text: The radius and ulna lie relatively parallel

questions.explanation: In supination the radius and ulna are relatively parallel and the palm faces anteriorly in anatomical position. Pronation rotates the radius across the ulna; this dynamic relationship should be considered when comparing forearm radiographs acquired in different positions.

questions.question: Which structure should be distinguished from the carpal tunnel when evaluating ulnar-sided hand neuropathy?
questions.explanation: Guyon canal transmits the ulnar nerve and artery at the ulnar wrist, whereas the carpal tunnel transmits the median nerve and flexor tendons. This distinction helps localize nerve compression based on the affected nerve and the site of symptoms.

questions.question: Which imaging finding is most consistent with a normal unfused secondary ossification centre rather than an acute fracture?

options.text: A displaced cortical fragment crossing the joint surface
A smoothly corticated ossicle in a typical developmental location
A newly visible fracture line through the main cortex
A sharp non-corticated fragment with acute soft-tissue swelling in the injury setting

correctAnswer.text: A smoothly corticated ossicle in a typical developmental location

questions.explanation: A normal accessory ossicle generally has smooth, corticated margins and a characteristic location, whereas an acute fracture more often has a sharp non-corticated edge and compatible trauma findings. The chapter emphasizes recognizing unfused ossification centres to avoid misdiagnosis.

questions.question: Which imaging technique is most appropriate for evaluating the bony detail of a complex shoulder fracture with multiplanar reconstructions?
questions.explanation: CT provides detailed depiction of complex bone anatomy and allows multiplanar and 3D reconstructions, which can clarify fracture fragments and articular involvement. Ultrasound and MRI have complementary roles for associated soft-tissue injury but do not replace CT for fine bony detail in selected complex fractures.

questions.question: Which forearm nerve is particularly associated with the pronator teres interval?
questions.explanation: The median nerve passes between the heads of pronator teres as it enters the forearm. This relationship is relevant to proximal forearm nerve entrapment and distinguishes its course from the ulnar nerve, which passes behind the medial epicondyle before entering the forearm.

questions.question: Which structure is the principal fibrocartilaginous stabilizer mentioned for the ulnar side of the wrist?

options.text: Volar plate of the thumb only

questions.explanation: The triangular fibrocartilage complex stabilizes the distal radioulnar joint and supports the ulnar side of the wrist. Its fibrocartilaginous and ligamentous components are not well assessed on routine radiographs, so MRI may be required when symptoms suggest TFCC injury.

questions.question: Which structure lies between the greater and lesser tubercles of the humerus and is visible as a longitudinal groove?

options.text: Radial groove of the humeral shaft

questions.explanation: The intertubercular or bicipital groove separates the greater and lesser tubercles and contains the long head of biceps tendon. It is a key proximal humeral landmark on radiographs, CT and MRI.

questions.question: Which ligament is associated with the coracoid process and acromion to form the coracoacromial arch?
questions.explanation: The coracoacromial ligament spans the coracoid process and acromion, completing the coracoacromial arch over the humeral head. The arch forms the superior boundary of the subacromial passage, where the supraspinatus tendon and bursa may be compressed.

questions.question: Which statement best explains why sonography is not equally effective for every upper-limb structure?

options.text: Ultrasound is restricted to internal abdominal organs
Bone obscures structures lying deep to it, although superficial soft tissues are well shown

correctAnswer.text: Bone obscures structures lying deep to it, although superficial soft tissues are well shown

questions.explanation: Ultrasound excels at superficial soft tissues but sound waves are blocked or attenuated by bone, limiting assessment of structures deep to osseous surfaces. MRI or CT may be better suited when the target is intra-articular, deeply situated or obscured by bone.

questions.question: Which wrist measurement is assessed in the coronal plane and reflects the distal radius surface slope toward the ulna?
questions.explanation: Ulnar inclination (ulnar slant) is assessed on the PA wrist view and reflects the coronal orientation of the distal radial articular surface. Palmar tilt is assessed on the lateral view and describes the sagittal orientation of the articular surface.

questions.question: Which wrist measurement is assessed on the lateral view and reflects the distal radial surface orientation in the sagittal plane?
questions.explanation: Palmar tilt, also called palmar inclination, describes the sagittal-plane orientation of the distal radial articular surface. It is distinct from ulnar inclination, which is assessed in the coronal plane on the PA view.

questions.question: Which joint is primarily responsible for flexion and extension at the wrist between the forearm and proximal carpal row?
questions.explanation: The radiocarpal joint links the distal radius and articular disc region with the proximal carpal row and permits wrist flexion-extension and deviation. Forearm pronation-supination occurs at the radioulnar joints rather than at the radiocarpal joint.

questions.question: Which structure is the principal bony articulation of the shoulder with the scapula for upper-limb movement?
questions.explanation: The glenohumeral joint is the main articulation between the humerus and scapula and provides extensive movement of the upper limb. The sternoclavicular and acromioclavicular joints connect and position the shoulder girdle, but they do not articulate the humeral head with the scapula.

questions.question: Which structure lies on the posterior aspect of the scapula and divides it into supra- and infraspinous fossae?
questions.explanation: The spine of the scapula is a prominent posterior ridge dividing the supraspinous and infraspinous fossae. It continues laterally as the acromion and serves as a landmark for the attachment and position of adjacent shoulder muscles.

questions.question: Which soft-tissue structure covers the humeral head and glenoid and contributes to the glenohumeral joint enclosure?
questions.explanation: The glenohumeral joint is enclosed by a capsule that attaches around the glenoid and proximal humerus. The capsule is reinforced by ligaments and related soft tissues, while the labrum deepens the socket and the rotator cuff contributes dynamic stability.

questions.question: Which imaging plane is especially useful for showing the relationship of the humeral head to the glenoid in an axial shoulder image?

options.text: Only a coronal plane of the pelvis

questions.explanation: Axial shoulder imaging shows the anterior-posterior relationship of the humeral head and glenoid and can help assess dislocation and associated anatomy. Coronal and sagittal planes add complementary information, especially for rotator cuff and labral assessment.

questions.question: Which structure of the proximal ulna projects anteriorly and contributes to the trochlear notch?
questions.explanation: The coronoid process projects anteriorly from the proximal ulna and forms part of the trochlear notch that articulates with the humeral trochlea. It is distinct from the posterior olecranon, which occupies the olecranon fossa during extension.

questions.question: Which anatomical structure is a key soft-tissue landmark in the anterior shoulder between the coracoid process and humerus?
questions.explanation: The coracohumeral ligament extends from the coracoid region toward the humerus and contributes to the superior capsular support around the shoulder. It is included among the structures visible in shoulder MRI and relates to the biceps pulley/rotator interval region.

questions.question: Which statement about the rotator cuff is most consistent with the chapter’s shoulder imaging emphasis?

options.text: It is located around the wrist
Its tendons are best assessed with ultrasound or MRI rather than plain radiography alone
Its tendons are bones visible only on radiographs

correctAnswer.text: Its tendons are best assessed with ultrasound or MRI rather than plain radiography alone

questions.explanation: The rotator cuff tendons surround the glenohumeral joint and help stabilize the humeral head. Ultrasound and MRI depict these soft tissues far better than plain radiography, and ultrasound additionally allows dynamic assessment during shoulder movement.

questions.question: Which structure is on the medial side of the elbow and is palpable as the inner epicondyle?
questions.explanation: The medial epicondyle is the prominent medial projection of the distal humerus and provides attachment for the common flexor origin and related ligamentous structures. The ulnar nerve passes immediately posterior to it, making the region clinically important after trauma.

questions.question: Which statement about carpal bones and imaging is most accurate?

options.text: Their overlapping shapes and small size make systematic review of alignment important
They are all arranged in a single row
They are not visible on radiographs

correctAnswer.text: Their overlapping shapes and small size make systematic review of alignment important

questions.explanation: The eight carpal bones are arranged in proximal and distal rows, and their small size and overlapping contours make systematic review important. PA and lateral views assess overall alignment, while CT or MRI may be needed for subtle fractures or ligamentous injury.

questions.question: Which structure forms the palmar boundary over the flexor tendons and median nerve at the wrist?
questions.explanation: The flexor retinaculum spans the carpal arch and forms the roof of the carpal tunnel. The extensor retinaculum is dorsal and retains extensor tendons in their compartments, so the two retinacula occupy opposite sides of the wrist.

questions.question: Which nerve is most directly associated with carpal tunnel syndrome?

options.text: Radial nerve at the spiral groove

questions.explanation: Carpal tunnel syndrome results from compression of the median nerve beneath the flexor retinaculum. The ulnar nerve follows a different route through Guyon canal, while the axillary and radial nerves are associated with more proximal regions of the upper limb.

questions.question: Which statement about upper-limb MRI is correct?

options.text: It is used only for cortical bone
It is unable to show tendons
It offers high soft-tissue contrast and can show structures in multiple planes

correctAnswer.text: It offers high soft-tissue contrast and can show structures in multiple planes

questions.explanation: MRI provides multiplanar soft-tissue contrast and can depict tendons, ligaments, muscle, marrow and joint fluid. Its role complements radiography and CT for bone and ultrasound for accessible superficial structures and dynamic evaluation.

questions.question: Which statement about CT and ultrasound is correct for upper-limb imaging?

options.text: Neither can depict the upper limb
Ultrasound is best for every structure deep to bone
CT is strong for detailed bone anatomy; ultrasound is strong for superficial dynamic soft tissues
CT is the only modality that shows tendons dynamically

correctAnswer.text: CT is strong for detailed bone anatomy; ultrasound is strong for superficial dynamic soft tissues

questions.explanation: CT provides detailed bony anatomy and 3D reconstruction, whereas ultrasound has high spatial resolution for superficial tendons and ligaments and allows dynamic assessment. Choosing between them depends on whether the question concerns bone, superficial soft tissue or motion.

questions.question: Which region of the proximal humerus is separated from the shaft by the surgical neck?
questions.explanation: The surgical neck lies distal to the humeral head and tubercles at the transition to the shaft. It is a clinically important fracture site because the axillary nerve and circumflex humeral artery pass around it.

questions.question: Which statement best describes the anatomical neck of the humerus?

options.text: It articulates with the radial head
It separates the humeral head from the tubercles
It separates the greater and lesser tubercles

correctAnswer.text: It separates the humeral head from the tubercles

questions.explanation: The anatomical neck forms the boundary between the articular humeral head and the tubercles. The bicipital groove separates the greater and lesser tubercles, while the surgical neck is more distal and is associated with neurovascular risk in fracture.

questions.question: Which joint allows the clavicle to articulate with the acromion of the scapula?
questions.explanation: The acromioclavicular joint connects the lateral clavicle with the acromion. It allows small gliding and rotational movements that help position the scapula, and injury may be assessed by evaluating alignment on shoulder radiographs.

questions.question: Which anatomical landmark on the scapula forms the socket for the humeral head and is bordered by the labrum?
questions.explanation: The glenoid fossa is the articular socket for the humeral head and is bordered by the glenoid labrum. The supraspinous and infraspinous fossae are posterior muscular surfaces divided by the scapular spine, not articular sockets.

questions.question: Which region of the elbow contains the brachial artery as it approaches its division into radial and ulnar arteries?
questions.explanation: The cubital fossa is an anterior elbow region containing important neurovascular structures, including the brachial artery near its division into radial and ulnar arteries. Its contents and boundaries are important for vascular access, trauma and cross-sectional anatomy.

questions.question: Which answer best explains the role of 3D reconstruction in upper-limb CT?

options.text: It allows complex bone surfaces and fracture fragments to be inspected from different angles
It provides dynamic tendon movement in real time

correctAnswer.text: It allows complex bone surfaces and fracture fragments to be inspected from different angles
